blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
HOLD TO SOUND DOCTRINE
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 1:1-20
This quarter we study into the close association of Paul and Timothy, a relationship which was never broken.

The Book of First Timothy was written by Paul to Timothy, a young minister of the Gospel of Christ. Paul wrote the letter for the purpose that Timothy would be encouraged and strengthened in holding to the sound doctrine of Christ as he had taught him. Paul, in stirring the spirit of Timothy, lays before each follower of Christ the truth that the work of the church must be done through the gifts of the Spirit. Leaders must be called of God and be examples of godly living.

Timothy had been called to the work of the ministry and had been given the necessary gift of the Spirit by which to carry it on. Paul's confidence in him was not disappointed. His letters to Timothy show affection, esteem, and trust. To the Philippians, he said of him, I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state (Philippians 2:19-23). We must hold fast to the truth of Christ and refuse false teachings.
MEMORY VERSE: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.—3 John 4
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 55 Promise of salvation.
Tue.—John 6:26-51 Doctrine of Jesus.
Wed.—Hebrews 6:1-8 Danger of falling.
Thu.—Hebrews 12:1-15 Steadfastness.
Fri.—2 John Abiding in the truth.
Devotional Reading: Colossians 2 —Be established in the truth.
The Relationship of Saints

1 Timothy 1:1-2 In the warm greeting of Paul to Timothy which opens this letter, we see that each occupied a genuine abiding place in the church, the body of Christ—Paul was an apostle of Jesus Christ, Timothy, my own son in the faith. Each entered his position by the spiritual act of God—Paul, by the commandment of God, Timothy, a son in the faith. And they were bound together in a close fellowship of love. These three characteristics are present in the Church of God.

The relationship of saints one to another is spiritual, and it is real. It is the closest union humans have with each other. Saints are related by the blood of Christ, born of the same Father, possessed of the same Spirit. They are branches growing on the same Vine. The world knows nothing of such. Clubs and so-called churches may have a business and social relationship, but no kinship, no spiritual fellowship, and no joy in one another such as the church has.

1 Timothy 1:3-4 Paul left Timothy at Ephesus while he went on to Macedonia. The Ephesian church was slipping from the state of purity they had when Paul wrote of his thankfulness for their faith and love and said they trusted in Christ and were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise (Ephesians 1:12-16). They had begun to leave their first love, a state described by Christ in Revelation 2:1-7. False teachers and bad examples were among them. Timothy must teach them to hold to true doctrine. Some evils which had crept in were fables—groundless legends, traditions, and opinions and genealogies—tracings of ancestry back to Abraham and tribal leaders. These had no basis in Scripture or authority from God. Such minister questions—raise disputes, doubts, separations over opinions. The opposite of this is godly edifying which is in faith. Progress in godliness can come only by way of faith—believing in God's Word and obeying it.

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
A Program of Love

1 Timothy 1:5-10 Paul pointed Timothy to the end of the commandment—the goal of God's dealings with man. The purpose of God's relation to man shown in the Law and the Prophets and completed in the atoning work of Christ is charity—the love of God filling the heart of man. God IS love. This love radiates out. It comes out of a pure heart. Love comes out of a good conscience, made good when sin is forgiven. It comes out of faith unfeigned—unpretended, genuine—for faith is necessary to receive God or any of His gifts. Thus faith, a clear conscience, and a pure heart are steps to reaching the experience God plans for us. Some have missed it because they have turned aside unto vain jangling—useless words, arguing, contention, trying to teach things they do not understand. Paul names things that are contrary to sound doctrine in verses 8-11.
Paul's Testimony

1 Timothy 1:11-17 Being reminded of the glorious Gospel, Paul begins to testify of what that Gospel has meant to his life. (1) It was Christ, not Paul himself, who put him into his place of service. God filled him with faith and love, that which is in Christ Jesus. (2) Paul tells of his former life while in sin—blasphemer . . . persecutor . . . injurious. Paul owned to being the chief of sinners. (3) Paul obtained mercy, because he did it ignorantly. He thought he was doing right (Acts 26:9). As soon as Paul knew the truth, he obeyed it (Acts 26:19). (4) Christ's mission to the world was to save sinners. (5) Paul obtained mercy so that Christ might shew forth all longsuffering—might demonstrate His saving work—for a pattern, or example, to them which should hereafter believe on him—on Christ—to life everlasting. (6) Then Paul breaks forth in thanks and praise to the God Who had done all this. He calls Him King eternal—Ruler of all forever; immortal— deathless, incorruptible; invisible—not seen, yet He is strongly felt in His works; only wise God—none beside Him. Paul gave Him honor and glory forever and ever— endlessly.
A Charge to Timothy

1 Timothy 1:18-20 This charge I commit unto thee—the work for which Paul left Timothy in Ephesus, to teach the church to hold to true doctrine and avoid false teachings. Timothy was to carry it on according to the prophecies—according to the spiritual gift and the instructions for its use which God gave him (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6-9). Prophecies are Words from God. Timothy was to war a good warfare. He was to hold faith, and a good conscience. Others, neglecting to do so, made shipwreck of their souls. Two names of individuals who had done so are named here. The delivering unto Satan is a punishment for blasphemy against the leading of the Holy Spirit in their lives. That they may learn. What a tragic lesson! Are we treating sin too lightly when we think we can have forgiveness whenever we ask it, regardless of our previous knowledge?
JUST A THOUGHT
A lame man on the right road will beat a fast man on the wrong road.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 2
PAUL TEACHES PRAYER HABITS
Scripture Text: 1Timothy 2:1-8

Paul wrote to pass on to Timothy what the Holy Spirit and experience had taught him of what a minister should be and of what the church should be. He urged Timothy to be always loyal to the doctrine of Christ, faithful to the call of God, and to pray much. He was to lead and teach the church as God led him. Prayer had a very important place in this. All saints should pray for all people from pure, holy hearts.

The church needed these teachings in all of its history, but, perhaps, never more than now. Present decay of moral standards, lukewarmness, and paganism in much of the religious world and the increasing encroachment by evil forces point up our need for the admonitions of Paul. As we study 1 Timothy, we will find many subjects of vital importance to the church today.
MEMORY VERSE: The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.—James 5:16b
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Judges 6:36-40 Seeking God's will.
Tue.—2 Kings 20:1-11 Hezekiah’s prayer.
Wed.—Psalm 5 A prayer of David.
Thu.—Daniel 9:1-22 Daniel’s prayer of confession.
Fri.—Matthew 7:7-11; John 16:23-27 God's prayer promise.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 6:5-15 Manner of praying.
Pray for All Men

1 Timothy 2:1-4 I exhort therefore—therefore always refers back to something before as the reason for making the present statement. Just before, Paul had urged Timothy to hold true to the faith of Christ. Some had made shipwreck by putting away this faith. For one way to avoid such disaster, Paul exhorted to prayer first of all—most important. Supplications—prayers for protection from evils or removal of troubles. Prayers—asking for the supply of one's own needs, spiritual or material. Intercessions—asking for the supply of needs of others. Giving of thanks—thanksgiving and praise to God for all that He is and all that He does for us and for others. These cover all the phases of Christian prayer. Prayer should be made for all men.

For kings, and for all that are in authority—All of us are dependent upon government. We should ask God to guide rulers and leaders, give them wisdom, incline their hearts and minds toward Him, prosper their good acts, and guard them from wrong ones. The granting of such prayers will produce better conditions in our world. Praying for all men and for rulers is good and acceptable in the sight of God. Surely, saints will do it, for they want, above all, to please God as well as to gain the other benefits. God wants these prayers because He desires all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. Prayers of the saints are cooperation with God. Their prayers can actually influence the quality of government.
One Universal Remedy

1 Timothy 2:5-6 One mediator Who is a ransom for all—ONLY one, but enough to save EVERY person. A mediator makes peace between, and joins together. Sin separates God and man. Jesus gave himself a ransom on the Cross to take away the enmity, the sins, and join God and the cleansed sinner together as Father and son

LESSON 2

or daughter. God wills that all be saved. He makes the way for all to be saved. This is the reason for our praying for all men. Praying releases the power of God to save souls and to work all kinds of good.

Christ gave Himself a ransom to be testified—witnessed— in due time. Since the gift is for all, all must be told. (See Acts 1:8.) This is the basis for all Christian work. We read in Proverbs 11:30 that he that wins souls is wise. This wisdom comes by prayer.
Paul's Place in the Church

1 Timothy 2:7 Paul was one witness. Whereunto—to the task of carrying the news of Christ's atonement to all—I am ordained—set apart, chosen. God chose Paul as a preacher—a proclaimer— and an apostle—one sent to new places with a message—a teacher of the Gentiles (Acts 9:15; Acts 26:16-18). Paul's message was in faith and verity, or in Spirit and truth. It was not vague, no mere "social gospel" or moral and economic uplift. It was of Jesus Christ, the one mediator and ransom for all. Paul was sure of his calling (I speak the truth . . . lie not). God has a definite work for each one now (1 Corinthians 12:18).

Paul said, "I am ordained a preacher." This was not the formal ordination of a human committee or board passing Paul's credentials and authorizing him to preach. It was not even the approval of his brethren and the laying on of their hands. God chose Paul (Acts 9:15). He laid out the work he was to do. God made him a minister and a witness. blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 3
THE CONDUCT OF WOMEN
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 2:9-15

When either women or men spend much time, cost, and attention on decorating themselves, they reveal that they have a lack within and that they are trying to supply that lack by the aids of dress and adornment.

What effect does the dress of women have upon their spirituality? How does it affect others? What is the best adornment? In what ways are the positions of men and women in the church equal? In what ways are they different?
Paul, in today's lesson, gives answers to these questions and teaches that God is no respecter of persons— male or female.
MEMORY VERSE: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel.—1 Peter 3:3
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—2 Kings 22 Huldah the prophetess.
Tue.—Luke 2:36-38; Acts 2:14-18; Acts 21:9 Women prophesied.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 14:1-6 Prophesying described.
Thu.—Galatians 3:26-29 All are one in Christ.
Fri.—1 Peter 3:1-9 Instructions to wives.
Devotional Reading: Proverbs 31:10-31 The virtuous woman.
Dress and Adornment

1 Timothy 2:9-10 In like manner also—like men were instructed in the preceding verse. They were instructed to pray in holiness, love, and faith. Out of the same kind of saintly lives, women are to adorn themselves. God loves beauty. Witness the exquisite and varied beauty He has lavished upon nature. To please Him, it must be true beauty, must be spiritual beauty of the heart and soul, not outer veneer or artificial decoration. See Isaiah 60:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:21. Paul speaks of the negative first. The adornment must not be that of broided hair—hair braided and entwined with gold, silver, etc. Gold …pearls…costly array. These are outward, material, perishable things. Instead, Paul turns to the positive side. Women must dress in modest apparel—decent, chaste, reserved, not bold, inconspicuous dress that covers the body without calling undue attention to either the person or the apparel. With shamefacedness—a desire to avoid anything alluring, extreme, flashy, or immodest. Without pride. Modest women dislike calling attention to themselves. Sobriety— with moderation, serious-mindedness, and simplicity. Clothing should not be extravagant either in expense or in style. It should be becoming, neither slovenly nor showy. It should be worn as a covering, not as a means of exciting admiration.

God desires His children to be adorned with good works. These add beauty to men and women professing godliness. Good works outside are produced by a good spirit inside. God sees as an ornament of great price, a meek and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:3-4). To His church, God says, Put on thy beautiful garments (Isaiah 52:1). God not only tells us what adornment to leave off, but He tells us what to put on to please Him.

The Bible does not prescribe details of styles and materials of dress, but it does set standards by which we can regulate our dress. It does not hold us to uniform attire. Dress can have much to do with feeding sinful pride. Saints should not dress and allow their children to dress as the world in shorts, halters, bathing suits, etc. God has but one standard for both.
© 2015 Church of God, Inc. The Conduct of Women─ Lesson 3 www.GodsAcres.org
SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 3
Woman's Place of Service

1 Timothy 2:11-12 Silence with all subjection. In what respect is this enjoined upon women? Paul makes it more clearly in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35. Brethren are to take the lead; sisters are to follow. Both Jewish and civil Roman law forbade women from doing what belonged especially to men. That women were acting in a disrespectful manner seems evident—they were to be in subjection, not to usurp authority (to boss), to be under obedience. Usurp means to take possession of without right or by force. Their speaking seems to have been asking questions, disputing, and disrupting in public assemblies—if they will learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. Women had been held back and deprived of assembly gatherings; they did not know how to conduct themselves. Paul was not saying that women could not preach or teach God's message. We read in both the Old and New Testaments of women who prophesied. (See Daily Readings.) The Holy Spirit was poured out upon both men and women. Read Acts 2:16-18; Joel 2:28-29. Prophesying by women appears to have been common. Paul deals with it in 1 Corinthians 11:5. In Philippians 4:3 Paul speaks of those women which labored with me in the gospel.

Would God have given to women the gift of prophecy or of teaching and the burden of using it and led them into places of service if He did not will that they use it? What does it signify that all of the twelve Apostles and authors of the Bible Books were men? In times past, most leadership was given to men, but women have been called by God to preach too. The brethren in places of leadership will not impose unjust or painful restrictions upon the sisters in Christ. Nor will the sisters, in exercising the gifts God has given them, depart from the womanly character of modesty, meekness, and gentleness. A woman filling the place to which God has called her is not usurping authority; that authority has been given to her rightfully. Neither men nor women should attempt to choose their work without the call of God, but having been placed by Him (1 Corinthians 12:18), each should fill that place as He leads.
The Influence of Eve

1 Timothy 2:13-15 Adam was first formed . . . was not deceived— was not the one misled by Satan into sin. Eve was deceived into eating the forbidden fruit and first to sin (Genesis 2:18, 22; Genesis 3:6). These two facts are given as the reason for the subjection of women to men. Does this subjection extend to the point where women are denied salvation? No. She shall be saved in child-bearing. Does motherhood save one? No. Only faith in Christ saves. "Saved in childbearing." Salvation came through a Child that was born because Jesus was the seed of Eve (Genesis 3:15) and was born of a woman, Mary (Galatians 4:4-5). Jesus became the Savior by Whom all must be saved, if at all, both men and women, for there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). Women as well as men are saved if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety. Jesus gave women freedom they had never known before.
JUST A THOUGHT
God is in the cleansing business not the white-washing business.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 2:9-10 In like manner also—like men were instructed in the preceding verse. They were instructed to pray in holiness, love, and faith. Paul speaks of the negative first. The adornment must not be that of broided hair—hair braided and entwined with gold, silver, etc. Gold …pearls…costly array. paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 2:11-12 Silence with all subjection. In what respect is this enjoined upon women? Paul makes it more clearly in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35. Brethren are to take the lead; sisters are to follow. Both Jewish and civil Roman law forbade women from doing what belonged especially to men. Their speaking seems to have been asking questions, disputing, and disrupting in public assemblies—if they will learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. Women had been held back and deprived of assembly gatherings; they did not know how to conduct themselves. Paul was not saying that women could not preach or teach God's message. We read in both the Old and New Testaments of women who prophesied. (See Daily Readings.) The Holy Spirit was poured out upon both men and women. Read Acts 2:16-18; Joel 2:28-29. Prophesying by women appears to have been common. Paul deals with it in 1 Corinthians 11:5. In Philippians 4:3 Paul speaks of those women which labored with me in the gospel.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 4
CHARACTER OF A BISHOP
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 3:1-7
A bishop or elder must be a true Christian in every way— toward his home, the church, and the world.

Are elders chosen or are they placed? Both. In all of God's work in the world, there is an inner current between God and man, a mutual working, a spiritual unity. God places certain abilities in a person. He has a desire to use that ability for good. He yields his life to God. He prays for spiritual gifts, always submissive to God's will. God gives; the man exercises and develops. God calls and places. Just how He works it all, we cannot tell, but there is a divine harmony in it which is beautiful to see. It brings true success in God's work and joy to the worker (1 Corinthians 12:18).
MEMORY VERSE: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially they who labor in the word and doctrine.—1 Timothy 5:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Ezekiel 33:1-16 Responsibility of a pastor.
Tue.—Acts 20:17-38 Paul counsels the elders.
Wed.—Ephesians 4:7-16 Gifts for perfecting the church.
Thu.—1 Thessalonians 2:1-12 In trust with the Gospel.
Fri.—1 Peter 5 An elder and his flock.
Devotional Reading: Titus 1:1-9 To ordain elders.
Desiring Spiritual Gifts

1 Timothy 3:1 If a man desire the office of a bishop— this is a rightful desire. Covet earnestly the best gifts—gifts of the Spirit to fit one for service. Desire spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:31; 1 Corinthians 14:1). Elder designates the rank or position. Originally meaning older, it is used to mean leading or superior. Bishop and pastor denote the functions. Bishop means overseer or superintendent. Pastor means one who feeds the flock, a shepherd. The same men are called elders and bishops in Titus 1:5, 7. Pastors are used in Ephesians 4:11. He desireth a good work. It is good to lead, teach, and bring to Christ, feed spiritually, protect, comfort, encourage, and build up the flock of God. There is a great need for more to desire this work. It is good both in what it accomplishes and in the rewards it brings to the doer. But every privilege brings its responsibilities.

Are all elders who are called elders? Many are trying to fill the position that are neither qualified nor called of God. What is wrong? They were appointed or elected by man rather than by God. We cannot make one an elder or bishop by electing him. God must both call and place him. We are told to desire, even covet, spiritual gifts and office, preferring that of prophecy. Our Scripture lists the requirements for being a bishop or elder. For clarity, let us number them in order and divide them according to the phase of life covered.
Personal Character

1 Timothy 3:2-3 (1) A bishop then must be blameless—a clear connection with God, justified, righteous, holy, one against whom no blame can be rightly laid. (2) The husband of one wife— one at a time, not a bigamist. An elder is not required to be married. Paul was not. However, he was not a settled pastor except for limited times, rather an apostle and evangelist. Yet, does not Christian marriage make a good pastor a better one
© 2015 Church of God, Inc. Character of a Bishop─ Lesson 4 www.GodsAcres.org

LESSON 4

by improving his effectiveness and providing him a help mate? (3) Vigilant—watchful, attentive to duty and to the needs of the people. (4) Sober—of sound mind, wise in judgment, serious- minded, self-controlled. (5) Of good behavior—of orderly, right, courteous, and refined conduct. Silliness, rudeness, and inconsiderateness have no place in the work of God. (6) Given to hospitality—inclined to receive and entertain those away from home or in need. See Hebrews 13:1-3. (7) Apt to teach— both able and willing to communicate his knowledge to others, having clear understanding of the truths of God, and the ability to make them clear to others. He will use his ability both in preaching and in teaching publicly and privately. This necessitates constant study and prayer. He strives to master the Bible. (8) Not given to wine—a total abstainer from intoxicating beverages, and also, from tobacco and drugs. (9) No striker— not disposed to defend himself or his doctrine by force, not desiring to harm or destroy those who oppose him, no persecutor. (10) Patient—meeting suffering, hardness, or injustices with calmness, persevering in right, letting love overrule. (11) Not a brawler—quiet, peaceable, not contentious, not quarrelsome, not making noisy disturbance. (12) Not covetous—not desiring gain for himself, not desiring the things of others. (13) Not greedy of filthy lucre—unselfish, not preaching for money, not loving money for its own sake, no ill-gotten gains, not desiring money more than spiritual things.
Family Life

1 Timothy 3:4-5 (14) One that ruleth well his own house—takes the leadership of his family as a husband and father should. He does it well, is neither a slave driver nor indifferent. Having his children in subjection— requiring obedience from them, directing their actions, and knowing where they are and what they are doing. He will teach his children to be good examples, polite, and respectful of others and not be unruly. (15) With all gravity—with seriousness, thoughtfulness. He thinks of the children's needs physically, mentally, and spiritually. Because he loves them, he is careful to do his best to supply them. This is required because his home is a man's first responsibility, and if he know not how to rule his own house, neither can he care for the Church of God. The ability required is the same for both.
Experience

1 Timothy 3:6 (16) Not a novice—not a beginner or newly converted or inexperienced. How can one who does not yet know the way, lead others? How can one who has not yet learned, teach others? When he shows himself worthy and has enough experience to walk ahead of his people, let him lead them. A novice raised to leadership is in danger of the sin of pride, by which he will fall into the condemnation of the devil. Pride is a weakness most easily fallen into.
Community Reputation

1 Timothy 3:7 (17) He must have a good report of them which are without—respected by the unconverted world. Unsaved people will not feel fellowship with a saint will not understand or agree with him and may not like him, but his life must be so upright that they will respect it and call it good. If it is otherwise, he will bring reproach—shame—upon himself and the church, fail to lead people to Christ, and will be caught in the snare of the devil—devil's trap. God does not have a double standard. The rules in our lesson for bishops and elders are for the rest of the church also. The same standard of holiness and perfection is given to us all.
JUST A THOUGHT
To hear truth and refuse it does not nullify truth.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 5
CHARACTER OF A DEACON
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 3:8-15

What is the authority of a deacon? Is it to work independently of the elder? Is it to hear from God and make clear His will to the people? Is it to take the offering, serve the Lord's Supper, or paint the building? He certainly has no authority in deciding matters such as calling a preacher or an evangelist to hold meetings. An elected trustee board, constituted to legally hold in trust the real estate and business affairs of the church, should be Spirit-led, but it can never rightly fill the place of God-ordained, Spirit-led elders and bishops. A deacon must be a true Christian in every way. We can find the answer to these questions in the Scripture in our lesson.
MEMORY VERSE: Likewise must the deacons be grave, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre. —1 Timothy 3:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Proverbs 16 Right use of speech.
Tue.—Matthew 25:31-40 Service to needy.
Wed.—Romans 16:1-16 Helpers in God's work.
Thu.—1 Peter 3:10-16 Upright Christian living.
Fri.—1 Peter 4:1-11 Serving God seriously.
Devotional Reading: 1 Corinthians 12 God sets offices in church.
Personal Qualifications of a Deacon

1 Timothy 3:8-10 Likewise must the deacons—in the same way as the elders. (See Lesson 4.) The word deacon means a regularly constituted servant. Deacons serve in much the same way as elders, but in a secondary capacity. We might call them assistants to elders. They are to carry more of the material service such as providing for the needs of the sick and poor, while elders look more to the spiritual needs. Yet, their service is the same in many respects. Their character must be as holy as an elder's, a good example for all to follow. (1) Must the deacons be grave—thoughtful, serious-minded, realizing the importance and responsibility of their call? Both thoughts and actions should be suitable for the seriousness of the position. (2) Not double-tongued— not talking on both sides of a subject, two-faced, hypocritical. (3) Not given to much wine—no drinker of intoxicants. How can a person given to God be also given to wine—sold, bound, enslaved? No man can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). (4) Not greedy of filthy lucre—not in it for financial gain. Money cannot satisfy, is perishable, and keeps one's eyes from the greater gain. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness (Matthew 6:33). Needs left in God's hands, He will supply. (5) Holding the mystery of the faith—understanding and believing the doctrine of Christ, His deity, death, resurrection, and what these accomplish for sinners. In a pure conscience—free from guilt, forgiven, saved, justified, and holy. Not only must deacons believe Christ's doctrine, but they must experience it. (6) Let these also first be proved—a newly-saved, inexperienced, untrained one is not ready. Let him learn, gain experience and understanding, be proved or tried. When he shows himself worthy and capable, let him use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 5
His Family Life

1 Timothy 3:11 Even so—out of the same kind of holy life—must their wives be—if wives are to help their husbands in spiritual work, they must be (a) grave—serious-minded about their work. (b) Not slanderers—not gossips, talebearers, breeders of suspicion, or evil-tongued. There is nothing more devilish than an evil tongue. Is any sin more easily fallen into than careless talking? Does any do more harm? (c) Sober— calm, steady, self-controlled, not giddy or silly. (d) Faithful in all things—true to Jesus Christ, dependable, trustworthy, honest in all dealings, sincere, constant. A pastor's wife of this sort is a great asset to any congregation.

1 Timothy 3:12 (7) Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife— true to marriage vows, not a bigamist. (8) Ruling their children and their own houses well—requiring obedience, not cruel, not slack, loving, teaching, training and directing his children, taking the headship of the family as the husband and father should, and guiding it in well-ordered ways.
Paul's Purpose in Writing

1 Timothy 3:13 They that have used the office of a deacon well— have followed the stated rules and been faithful to God— purchase to themselves a good degree—earn honor with both God and men, establish a good record—and great boldness in the faith—By practice and experience become learned in the Scriptures, wise in spiritual matters, able in teaching or preaching, powerful in prayer, and convincing to men. What greater reward can one seek in this life? There is no greater!

1 Timothy 3:14-15 Paul hopes to see Timothy soon, but in case of delay, he sent this letter of advice as to how best to conduct himself, or the best action to take to set the church in order. He uses three terms to designate the church. (1) The house of God— the temple in which God dwells. (Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:5.) These people in whom God lives are His church. (2) The church of the living God. (3) The pillar and ground of the truth. The truth is in both its foundation and its structure. The church grows out of the truth, and the church continues to lift and spread the truth. What a great responsibility the church has to hold high the truth that the world can see Christ, through Whom sinful souls are transformed into saints.
God's Perfect Plan of Church Government

The simple structure of the church as Christ set it up is perfect and entire, needing no addition or remodeling. He gives to each, gifts of the Spirit to carry on the work of the church. He sets elders and deacons to govern and direct the work. We find no higher human officers in the early church. These were led, taught, and guided by the Holy Spirit. There is no teaching in the Bible that men with superior authority should be set over the elders and congregations. (Matthew 20:25-26.) It was later when men, drifting from the Spirit's rule, set a bishop over elders, then an archbishop, and so on. The Pope of Rome was the first to take the title of Bishop of Bishops.
Deaconesses

In Romans 16:1 the word servant applied to Phoebe is the same term as is translated deacon in our lesson. The word deaconess is not in the Bible. What would be the work and standing of such a servant?
JUST A THOUGHT
"He that is at war with others is not at peace with himself."

LESSON 6
THE MYSTERY OF GODLINESS
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 Corinthians 2:7-12; Colossians 1:26-27; Ephesians 1:9-10

What is the mystery of godliness? By what means can we understand it? Is it important that we understand it? Does a person who has a Bible or a place of worship necessarily have the Gospel? Do living with Christians or attending Sunday school and preaching services guarantee that one knows the Gospel or understands the mystery? (1 Corinthians 2:14.) Does knowing the words of the Bible reveal to one the mystery? How does our text agree with the song that says, "It is no secret what God can do?"
Salvation is a mystery to those without God's Spirit. The mystery is that God's Son came, became flesh, died, rose, and returned to Heaven to save man from sin.

MEMORY VERSE: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. —1 Timothy 3:16
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Psalm 25 A prayer to be taught of God.
Tue.—Matthew 13:10-17, Matthew 13:35 Reason for parables.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 4:1-6 Gospel hid to the lost.
Thu.—Ephesians 1:1-12 Purpose of the mystery revealed.
Fri.—1 Peter 1:3-13, 1 Peter 1:20 The mystery revealed.
Devotional Reading: Ephesians 3 Mystery made known to Paul.
Great Is the Mystery

1 Timothy 3:16 Without controversy—certain, without possibility of refutation—great is the mystery— something secret, hidden, not known to all—of godliness—of Godlikeness, of making men like God. This is the greatest plan that concerns mankind. Paul names six details of how the plan will be carried out. (1) God was manifest in the flesh—Jesus Christ, or God the Son, became man. He took upon Himself a human body. The Word was made flesh (John 1:14). These statements prove the deity and also the humanity of Jesus. (2) Justified in the Spirit—was proven by the Holy Spirit to be what He claimed to be. At His baptism (John 1:32-34), His resurrection (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 3:18), and by His miracles (John 10:25), the Spirit justified Him. (3) Seen of angels—That angels have an interest and a part in the redemptive work of Christ is shown by their activity in preparation for His coming, at His birth, flight to Egypt, temptation, agony, resurrection, and ascension. They rejoice over one sinner that repenteth (Luke 15:10). They desire to look into these truths (1 Peter 1:12). (4) Preached unto the Gentiles—to non-Jews as well as Jews. It is a precious part of this mystery that Jesus tasted death for every man, not one left out (Hebrews 2:9). (5) Believed on in the world—among the unbelievers there are also those who believe everywhere Christ is preached. Sinners whose sins He denounces embrace Him as their Savior. (6) Received up into glory—ascended back to Heaven from where He came. This is all important to us. His living is the promise of our living (John 14:19). His entrance into Heaven is the promise of our entrance. His going with His visible, human body is the promise of our going with ours. His eternal living is the promise of ours. Praise God! These and more belong to the plan of salvation whereby sinful people are made godly. This is truly a mystery. The world cannot understand this.

LESSON 6
A Mystery to the Unsaved

1 Corinthians 2:7-8 But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom. Hidden because it is not understood. God's plan of salvation through Christ was ordained before the world—was planned by God before creation of the world. God gradually made it known through His Prophets, but they themselves did not fully understand what they wrote of Christ (Romans 16:25-26; 1 Peter 1:10-12). The fuller revelation came with the coming of Christ. None of the princes of this world knew—earthly, natural men, those out-side of Christ, did not know this mysterious wisdom, this plan of God (Mark 4:11). Thanks be to God! It can be known.
The Mystery Revealed by the Spirit

1 Corinthians 2: 9-12 The things which God hath prepared for them that love him—the blessings of salvation in this present life. Many separate verse 9 from verse 10 in the context and so misinterpret it. Man's natural eyes, ears, and heart cannot grasp these things, but God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit. The spirit of man knoweth the things of a man. The Spirit of God knoweth the things of God. God planned it this way. That is why He gave us the spirit which is of God—the Holy Spirit—that we might know the things that are freely given to us by God. Through the working of the Spirit, we can take His gift of salvation, can experience it, grow in it, know it, feel it, and know God and Jesus Christ. Knowing the mysteries, we hold them in our hearts. We are made stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1). As stewards, we are bound by love and duty to teach others.
The Substance of God's Plan

Colossians 1:26-27 The riches of the glory of this mystery . . . is Christ in you. The whole plan, from beginning to end, is to bring about the indwelling of Christ in the hearts of men. What a great mystery! God wants us to know this. He also wants us to know the purpose for which Christ dwells in us. God tells us the specific details of His plan that is great enough to occupy His attention from before the Creation until time shall cease. Then the mystery of God shall be finished, not ended, but complete (Revelation 10:7).
The Goal of God's Plan

Ephesians 1:9-10 The mystery of his will . . . that in . . . the fullness of times—this is the next dispensation which will begin at Christ's Second Coming when the world ends and time shall be no more—then He will gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth. All who have salvation will be brought together in one great family to dwell even in him. This includes God the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the angels, and all redeemed people. Then we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).
Oh, how great is the mystery of godliness! Dear friend, don't miss it. Start today. Make Christ your personal Savior.
JUST A THOUGHT
"Man gets and forgets; God gives and forgives." —Myron F. Boyd

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 7
PROPHECY OF COMING APOSTASY
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 4:1-9; Colossians 2:8, Colossians 2:13-23

The express speaking of the Spirit names specific practices which are the outgrowth of apostasy. Apostasy is the departure from true teaching and beliefs. What religious systems fit the description named in our text? Is Catholicism the only system that incurs God's wrath? Wherever men stray from the mainstream of the Gospel, God's attitude toward it and the result is the same. The tragic result brings a departing of God's Spirit from a group or an individual life. What would you call the chief wrong of the apostasy foretold here? What is meant by bodily exercise?
Apostasy in the latter times is prophesied. We must watch that we be not led astray.
MEMORY VERSE: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. —1 Thessalonians 5:21
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Proverbs 1:1-9 Where true wisdom is found.
Tue.—Jeremiah 23:1-6, Jeremiah 23:21-32 True and false prophets.
Wed.—Ezekiel 34:1-10 False shepherds.
Thu.—2 Peter 2:1-11 False teachers.
Fri.—2 Peter 3 The destiny of the false and the true.
Devotional Reading: Galatians 1— Some would pervert Gospel.
Some Shall Depart

1 Timothy 4:1-3 The Spirit speaketh expressly—the Holy Spirit spoke to Paul, pointedly, specifically, clearly. In the latter times—meaning later than He spoke, in the last dispensation, the one then in its beginning and now still continuing in these latter days—some shall depart from the faith—from the truth of Christ, the way of salvation. Why? Because they give heed to—listen to—seducing spirits—spirits that deceive— and doctrines of devils—evil teachings and practices. Paul names some: (1) Teaching about demons. Pagans worshipped demons believed to be agents between gods and men, some being souls of dead humans. This practice would be a part of the worship of those apostates. (2) Speaking lies in hypocrisy. Not being founded on truth, they do not love truth, but follow the devil's practice of lying (John 8:44). In hypocrisy—pretending to be good, wearing a cloak of right (Matthew 7:15-16). (3) Having their conscience seared with a hot iron. Deadened to feeling, they sin with no remorse and seemingly little realization that it is sin. They feel no repentance. The same hot iron of the Gospel of Christ that smoothes out the wrinkles of the hearer will sear the conscience if unheeded. (4) Forbidding to marry. Refusing themselves to marry and requiring others to remain single, forgetting God's Word that marriage is honorable in all (Hebrews 13:4). (5) Commanding to abstain from meats. They make rules forbidding food at certain times or certain foods to be eaten ever or at certain times.

LESSON 7
Freedom in Christ

1 Timothy 4:4-5 Every creature of God—everything created by God— is good. He called it very good (Genesis 1:31). Nothing to be refused—that is, nothing that was made for food is to be denied or forbidden—if received with thanksgiving. No ungrateful, arrogant reaching for God's gifts as if they belonged to us pleases God. If accepted thankfully, food is sanctified— pure and sacred. Two things make it so. (1) The word of God. God's Word or authority set food apart for man's use (Genesis 1:29). (2) And prayer—both prayer for God to provide (Matthew 6:11) and thanks to Him for having done so (Romans 14:6; Ephesians 5:20).
How to Be a Good Servant

1 Timothy 4:6 Timothy was put in trust by God as a minister, a servant of God and the church. To fulfill this trust, he must put the brethren in remembrance of these things—tell, remind, instruct, warn them of the coming apostasy and teach them how to refuse the false and hold to the truth. Thus Timothy would show himself nourished or taught in the words of faith and of good doctrine. Paul knew he had attained to this place and wanted him to continue in it.

Can one be a good servant of Christ and shut his eyes to the signs of apostasy? Can one be a good watchman and not warn the flock of these dangers? Can he be true to the Lord and the spiritual gift given him unless he puts the brethren in remembrance of the sharp line of difference between godliness and fables? It may make one popular to cooperate with everything and to smile at all doctrines, but it does not please God. See 2 Corinthians 6:14-16.
Godliness Versus Bodily Exercise

1 Timothy 4:7-9 Throughout our lesson text we see two ways of life expressed. They are (1) godliness, or Godlikeness, obeying God, living as motivated by the Spirit, and (2) bodily exercise, or outward forms and observances, obeying man's ordinances, living as motivated by our minds and wills. The first is freedom in Christ (John 8:36); the second is bondage to man's rules. The first is on the inside; the second, on the outside. The first is minding the things of the Spirit; the second, minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5). The first is living in the power of God; the second is living in one's own human strength. Godliness is profitable unto all things. Godliness benefits in this life and also in the life to come. But bodily exercise profiteth little—is wasted effort. Refuse profane and old wives' fables—earthly, man-made traditions and superstitions. They lead many souls to destruction.

Colossians 2:8, Colossians 2:13-23 Even the forms and days of the Mosaic Law are of no effect since Christ came. They were the shadow or type. Christ is the body or real substance, the antitype. Voluntary humility is much the same as bodily exercise. By their own willpower, people afflict the physical body in outward, material ways. They forbid touching or tasting or handling. They neglect or punish the body to gain merit. They spend their time and energy on things that are to perish with the using— outward things. They forget the Head, Christ. They neglect inward things of the Spirit. This has a show of wisdom, looks very religious, but does not bring freedom or satisfy the longing in the heart, and has no value to the saving of the soul.
Lies and Hypocrisy

The magazine, Christian Heritage of June 1959, quotes Catholic sources as teaching, "For a grave reason, a lie may be told without sin to a person who has no right to the truth." One whose writings are taught in Roman Catholic seminaries lists many examples of excusable lying. Their forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats is well known. Trust in bodily exercise or voluntary humility is evident in their great use of dress, learned prayers, observance of days, images, shrines, beads, charms, penance, candles, crosses, etc. All

these are on the outside and of little profit. They do not reach the heart where true godliness must be. It is trusting in one's own efforts rather than in Christ's atonement." Some shall depart from the faith" refers to any and all who turn from Christ and His Word to another doctrine.
JUST A THOUGHT
Salvation is much more than acknowledging God's power.

1 Timothy 4:1-3 The Spirit speaketh expressly—the Holy Spirit spoke to Paul, pointedly, specifically, clearly.

In the latter times—meaning later than He spoke, in the last dispensation, the one then in its beginning and now still continuing in these latter days—some shall depart from the faith—from the truth of Christ, the way of salvation.
Why?
Because they give heed to—listen to—seducing spirits—spirits that deceive— and doctrines of devils—evil teachings and practices.
Paul names some: (1) Teaching about demons.
Pagans worshipped demons believed to be agents between gods and men, some being souls of dead humans.
This practice would be a part of the worship of those apostates. (2) Speaking lies in hypocrisy.
Not being founded on truth, they do not love truth, but follow the devil's practice of lying (John 8:44).
In hypocrisy—pretending to be good, wearing a cloak of right (Matthew 7:15-16). (3) Having their conscience seared with a hot iron.
Deadened to feeling, they sin with no remorse and seemingly little realization that it is sin.
They feel no repentance.
The same hot iron of the Gospel of Christ that smoothes out the wrinkles of the hearer will sear the conscience if unheeded. (4) Forbidding to marry.
Refusing themselves to marry and requiring others to remain single, forgetting God's Word that marriage is honorable in all (Hebrews 13:4). (5) Commanding to abstain from meats.
They make rules forbidding food at certain times or certain foods to be eaten ever or at certain times.
1 Timothy 4:4-5 Every creature of God—everything created by God— is good.
He called it very good (Genesis 1:31).
Nothing to be refused—that is, nothing that was made for food is to be denied or forbidden—if received with thanksgiving.
No ungrateful, arrogant reaching for God's gifts as if they belonged to us pleases God.
If accepted thankfully, food is sanctified— pure and sacred.
Two things make it so. (1) The word of God.
God's Word or authority set food apart for man's use (Genesis 1:29). (2) And prayer—both prayer for God to provide (Matthew 6:11) and thanks to Him for having done so (Romans 14:6; Ephesians 5:20).
1 Timothy 4:6 Timothy was put in trust by God as a minister, a servant of God and the church.
To fulfill this trust, he must put the brethren in remembrance of these things—tell, remind, instruct, warn them of the coming apostasy and teach them how to refuse the false and hold to the truth.
Thus Timothy would show himself nourished or taught in the words of faith and of good doctrine.
Paul knew he had attained to this place and wanted him to continue in it.
Can one be a good servant of Christ and shut his eyes to the signs of apostasy?
Can one be a good watchman and not warn the flock of these dangers?
Can he be true to the Lord and the spiritual gift given him unless he puts the brethren in remembrance of the sharp line of difference between godliness and fables?
It may make one popular to cooperate with everything and to smile at all doctrines, but it does not please God.

1 Timothy 4:7-9 Throughout our lesson text we see two ways of life expressed.

They are (1) godliness, or Godlikeness, obeying God, living as motivated by the Spirit, and (2) bodily exercise, or outward forms and observances, obeying man's ordinances, living as motivated by our minds and wills.
The first is freedom in Christ (John 8:36); the second is bondage to man's rules.
The first is on the inside; the second, on the outside.
The first is minding the things of the Spirit; the second, minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5).
The first is living in the power of God; the second is living in one's own human strength.
Godliness is profitable unto all things.
Godliness benefits in this life and also in the life to come.
But bodily exercise profiteth little—is wasted effort.
Refuse profane and old wives' fables—earthly, man-made traditions and superstitions.
They lead many souls to destruction.
Colossians 2:8, Colossians 2:13-23 Even the forms and days of the Mosaic Law are of no effect since Christ came.
They were the shadow or type.
Christ is the body or real substance, the antitype.
Voluntary humility is much the same as bodily exercise.
By their own willpower, people afflict the physical body in outward, material ways.
They forbid touching or tasting or handling.
They neglect or punish the body to gain merit.
They spend their time and energy on things that are to perish with the using— outward things.
They forget the Head, Christ.
They neglect inward things of the Spirit.
This has a show of wisdom, looks very religious, but does not bring freedom or satisfy the longing in the heart, and has no value to the saving of the soul.
The magazine, Christian Heritage of June 1959, quotes Catholic sources as teaching, "For a grave reason, a lie may be told without sin to a person who has no right to the truth."
One whose writings are taught in Roman Catholic seminaries lists many examples of excusable lying.
Their forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats is well known.
Trust in bodily exercise or voluntary humility is evident in their great use of dress, learned prayers, observance of days, images, shrines, beads, charms, penance, candles, crosses, etc.
All these are on the outside and of little profit.
They do not reach the heart where true godliness must be.
It is trusting in one's own efforts rather than in Christ's atonement."
Some shall depart from the faith" refers to any and all who turn from Christ and His Word to another doctrine.
Salvation is much more than acknowledging God's power.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 8
ADVICE TO A YOUNG MINISTER
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 4:10-16

Why is it that so few of the modern ministers seem to never have seriously read these directions stated by Paul in today's lesson text? For most, their method of spending their time, the business and pleasures of their lives, and the objectives that they pursue cause them to be just the opposite of what they should be.

No other way is found in the New Testament for doing God's work than by God's spiritual gifts. 1 Corinthians 12:1 says we should not be ignorant about spiritual gifts. 1 Corinthians 12:18 says everyone is set in the body as God pleases. Each has a particular place with a particular work. 1 Peter 4:10-11 says that if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth. There is no other way to success in God's work. Timothy ministered by means of a gift of the Spirit. What is the way to obtain spiritual gifts?
MEMORY VERSE: Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.—1 Timothy 4:16
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Joshua 1:1-9 God's charge to Joshua.
Tue.—Ezekiel 33:1-9 Responsibility of watchmen.
Wed.—Matthew 10:16-33 Men of God can expect persecution.
Thu.—Acts 26:12-23 Paul's call to God's work.
Fri.—Romans 10 The need for God-sent preaching.
Devotional Reading: Romans 1:1-16 Ready to preach Gospel.
Laborers Suffer Reproach

1 Timothy 4:10-11 The first verse of this chapter told of a departure from the faith, from the great mystery of godliness. Paul exhorted Timothy to press on in the way of godliness, which promises great profit both in this life and in the next. For therefore—because we desire to preserve this way of godliness—we both labor and suffer reproach. Paul and others like him valued the Gospel of Christ so highly that they were glad to work and be persecuted severely because of their trust in the living God. Here the same One is called both God and Savior, one more proof of the deity of Jesus Christ. Jesus is the God and Savior of all men—He died for all (2 Corinthians 5:15), was crucified to draw all men unto Him (John 12:32), is the Light, which lighteth every man (John 1:9), and is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).

He is the Savior specially of those that believe. Only these actually receive salvation. Salvation is for all, but not all have it. Read Matthew 7:14; John 3:36. These verses should settle two false teachings, (1) Limited Atonement (that Christ died to save a limited part of mankind) and (2) Universalism (that everyone will be saved). No, the atonement is not limited, but acceptance of it is. God wills all to be saved, but not all will repent. These things command and teach. What things? That men should refuse false doctrine and pursue godliness, that godliness brings blessing both now and hereafter, that salvation in Christ is of so great value as to render unimportant any labor or persecution brought by it, and that Jesus saves from sin any and all who believe on Him.

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 8
Youth Is a Powerful Influence

1 Timothy 4:12-13 Let no man despise thy youth. Timothy was a young man, but he should not let his youth lead him into foolish, hasty, extreme, passionate, or worldly action. This would bring the criticism that he was too young to lead. Instead, he must be an example of the believers—show what an ideal believer is, that others might pattern after him. In word—in what he said and what he taught, teaching the truth, the Gospel of Christ. In conversation—in all of his conduct in all places at all times, act in a holy, Christian manner. In charity—let the love of God within him rule his conduct. In spirit—in the inward feeling and visible attitude in which he lived and acted. In faith—living continually with an open channel of trust reaching to God by which to communicate with Him and receive from Him. This also includes the thought of faithfulness to God and to the church in the trust placed in his hands. He must be a faithful steward of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1-2). In purity—unmixed with sin, sanctified unto God, unspotted from the world, clean in thought and action, giving no one reason to scandalize his good name.

Give attendance to reading—read the Bible, study it, let his delight be in the Law of the Lord; meditate on it every day. Give attendance to exhortation—pass on to the people the commands of God and the importance of obedience. And to doctrine—teach the people the truths of God, give them a solid foundation in God's Word from which to grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior (2 Peter 3:18).

All through Bible history, in both the Old and New Testaments, there have been young people whom God used in a mighty way. God does not consider the age of a person, but He looks at the willingness and obedience of those He would use in His work. Let no young person feel he is too young to be of service to God. Do not be intimidated because you are young when God has a work for you.
Serving and Continuing Faithful

1 Timothy 4:14 Neglect not the gift—the gift of the Spirit which God had placed in Timothy had (1) set him in his particular place of service in the church and (2) given the spiritual abilities necessary to do that work. Two actions accompanied the giving of this gift to Timothy, (1) prophecy—Word from God telling Timothy and others of His choice of Timothy for this work and (2) the laying on of the hands of Paul and other elders (1 Timothy 1:18; 2 Timothy 1:6). Paul urged Timothy to neglect not—to develop the gift by using it, by prayer, and listening to God.

1 Timothy 4:15-16 Meditate upon these things—think deeply and continually on the truths he read, the great salvation of which he was steward in the Gospel, his responsibility in leading the church and winning souls, the goals set before him, and the gift by which he did all. Give thyself wholly—not halfheartedly, but make the service of God his one interest and concern.

Two matters Timothy was told to take heed unto: First, thyself—pay careful attention to his own life that it please God, that he himself obey the Spirit and God's Word, and that his heart remain pure. Second, the doctrine—watch carefully to always teach God's Word as it is, the full Gospel, unmixed with error. These would bring two results: First, he would save himself; by remaining true to God, he would assure his final salvation in Heaven. Second, he would save those who heard him; his holy example and teaching of truth would bring them to God. God has chosen to give us His will in a Book. What are we doing with it?
JUST A THOUGHT
Reading is a priceless treasure and a powerful influence.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 4:10-11 The first verse of this chapter told of a departure from the faith, from the great mystery of godliness. Paul exhorted Timothy to press on in the way of godliness, which promises great profit both in this life and in the next. For therefore—because we desire to preserve this way of godliness—we both labor and suffer reproach. Paul and others like him valued the Gospel of Christ so highly that they were glad to work and be persecuted severely because of their trust in the living God. Here the same One is called both God and Savior, one more proof of the deity of Jesus Christ. Jesus is the God and Savior of all men—He died for all (2 Corinthians 5:15), was crucified to draw all men unto Him (John 12:32), is the Light, which lighteth every man (John 1:9), and is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).

paragraphs.text: He is the Savior specially of those that believe. Only these actually receive salvation. Salvation is for all, but not all have it. Read Matthew 7:14; John 3:36. These verses should settle two false teachings, (1) Limited Atonement (that Christ died to save a limited part of mankind) and (2) Universalism (that everyone will be saved). No, the atonement is not limited, but acceptance of it is. God wills all to be saved, but not all will repent. These things command and teach. What things? That men should refuse false doctrine and pursue godliness, that godliness brings blessing both now and hereafter, that salvation in Christ is of so great value as to render unimportant any labor or persecution brought by it, and that Jesus saves from sin any and all who believe on Him.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 4:12-13 Let no man despise thy youth. Timothy was a young man, but he should not let his youth lead him into foolish, hasty, extreme, passionate, or worldly action. This would bring the criticism that he was too young to lead. Instead, he must be an example of the believers—show what an ideal believer is, that others might pattern after him. In word—in what he said and what he taught, teaching the truth, the Gospel of Christ. In conversation—in all of his conduct in all places at all times, act in a holy, Christian manner. In charity—let the love of God within him rule his conduct. In spirit—in the inward feeling and visible attitude in which he lived and acted. In faith—living continually with an open channel of trust reaching to God by which to communicate with Him and receive from Him. This also includes the thought of faithfulness to God and to the church in the trust placed in his hands. He must be a faithful steward of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1-2). In purity—unmixed with sin, sanctified unto God, unspotted from the world, clean in thought and action, giving no one reason to scandalize his good name.

paragraphs.text: All through Bible history, in both the Old and New Testaments, there have been young people whom God used in a mighty way. paragraphs.text: Two matters Timothy was told to take heed unto: First, thyself—pay careful attention to his own life that it please God, that he himself obey the Spirit and God's Word, and that his heart remain pure. Second, the doctrine—watch carefully to always teach God's Word as it is, the full Gospel, unmixed with error. These would bring two results: First, he would save himself; by remaining true to God, he would assure his final salvation in Heaven. Second, he would save those who heard him; his holy example and teaching of truth would bring them to God. God has chosen to give us His will in a Book. What are we doing with it?

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 9
CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS IN SOCIETY
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 5:1-8; 1 Timothy 6:1-2

As we study, we should bear in mind that even though the Book of Timothy was written to a young pastor and is primarily advice for the carrying on of his work, it states the basic principles for the individual Christian's success in the society in which he lives. The only difference is in the particular circumstance in which each is placed. So here, while Timothy may have viewed these instructions from one position and some of us from another, still, they have an application for every one of us.

Christian attitudes of kindness, love, and respect must be used toward all people. We must provide for those for whose support we are responsible. Who has the first responsibility in the care of needy ones and dependents? What virtue is most effective in producing right relations between individuals?
MEMORY VERSE: Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. —Philippians 2:4
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Leviticus 19:30-37 Respect and justice.
Tue.—Psalm 78:1-8 Teaching children God's Law.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 13 The love of God in action.
Thu.—Ephesians 6:1-9 The Christian household.
Fri.—Colossians 3 Holy living.
Devotional Reading: Titus 2 Christian doctrine and conduct.
Treatment of Others

1 Timothy 5:1-2 Rebuke not—In correcting faults, wrongs, or misunderstandings, in what manner shall it be done? Gently, tenderly, with the love one would show to one's own brother, sister, father, or mother. If in the church, they are brothers and sisters, born of the same Father. Rebuke not . . . but entreat—with gentle understanding, seek to persuade them to a better way. An elder here means an older man, not a church officer. The term corresponds to the term elder women. These are to be given the loving respect due parents; the younger ones deserve respect due brothers and sisters in a family. With all purity—Timothy, as a young minister, must be especially careful in his conduct toward younger women, to avoid temptation to himself, temptation to them, and suspicion on the part of others. This same standard of respect should be maintained by all toward any of the opposite sex.
Caring for Relatives

1 Timothy 5:3-7 Honor widows that are widows indeed—accept and support those destitute of other support. This, obviously, is speaking to the church. Then, to individuals again—if any widow has children or nephews, let them assume the support. Thus they shew piety at home, which is a first duty, and requite their parents—repay for the love and care they received in their helpless years. Best of all, they please God. Then, two kinds of widows are contrasted—widows indeed and those who live in pleasure, in luxury, ease, and self-indulgence. The first trust in God, while the others do not. The first live by continual prayer. The second are

LESSON 9

dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), spiritually dead, while living physically. Material comforts and worldly pleasures dull the sense of dependence upon God. These things give in charge—teach to the people that they may obey and be blameless.

Today the increasing number of elderly people and the large number of working wives has brought a growth in the custom of placing elderly parents and relatives in nursing centers. Does this fulfill one's duty to them? How much weight should each of these bear upon the decision of what to do—The wife's job? The disposition of the aged one? Adults' desire for freedom? Finances? Size of house? What benefits may come to each household member when a dependent is cared for? To live in pleasure, in self-indulgence, and to please self is to be dead spiritually. This is true of an individual or a church or a nation.
Duty of Supporting Own Family

1 Timothy 5:8 A man must provide for his own—any relatives for whom he is the main means of support. Specially for those of his own house—his immediate family, wife, children, parents, or those under his roof. These are his first responsibility. Then he should reach to other dependents as far as he is able. To shirk his duty is to deny the faith, to sin against his Christian profession. Worse than an infidel or unbeliever, for even unbelievers generally fill their responsibility for their own.

This is part of the nurture and admonition of the Lord in which children should be brought up. Read Ephesians 6:4. This is part of our training them in respect for their elders, in faithful discharge of responsibilities, in self-sacrifice rather than self-indulgence. It is not fair to a child to let him grow up pampered and free from responsibility, then expect him to assume the duties of adulthood. The duties of our lesson are for adults and children alike.
Relation of Servants and Masters

1 Timothy 6:1-2 Should a saint be a servant under the yoke? Not under the yoke and bondage of slavery, but under the yoke of Jesus his Master. He should not rebel against serving those who have the authority over him. Such action would cause blasphemy or unjust criticism of God and his doctrine. We are not living in a day of slavery as when this letter was written, but this does not give reason for the saint to give less than his best to those for whom he is employed. He should give a full day's work for a full day's pay. The unsaved always watch Christians and expect a higher degree of patience and work ethics from them. If a master is a Christian also, the servant must not feel that his spiritual equality is reason for a lesser effort, or reason to take an advantage of him—despise them, because they are brethren. Rather, he must serve faithfully because his master is a beloved brother, a partaker of the benefit of salvation. Being united with him in Christ, he serves from love (Galatians 5:13). Work as unto the Lord and not to man. Read Ephesians 6:5-9.
JUST A THOUGHT
After a man makes his mark in the world, a lot of people will come around with erasers.

We are not living in a day of slavery as when this letter was written, but this does not give reason for the saint to give less than his best to those for whom he is employed. He should give a full day's work for a full day's pay. The unsaved always watch Christians and expect a higher degree of patience and work ethics from them. If a master is a Christian also, the servant must not feel that his spiritual equality is reason for a lesser effort, or reason to take an advantage of him—despise them, because they are brethren. Rather, he must serve faithfully because his master is a beloved brother, a partaker of the benefit of salvation. Being united with him in Christ, he serves from love (Galatians 5:13). Work as unto the Lord and not to man. Read Ephesians 6:5-9.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 10
CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS IN THE CHURCH
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 5:9-25

The choice of who should support the needy in Paul's day was between the church and relatives. It seems that governments of that time had no welfare programs. Care for the unfortunate is a product of love and is a peculiarity of God's people. Some governments have now taken over much welfare work. This is good and bad. Good, in that there are many needy ones who the church cannot help materially. But bad, in that the church has often been satisfied to leave it to them. There are some who are the government's responsibility. There are others who are the responsibility of relatives. But the church is responsible for its own. The church should provide for its needy ones, respect and support its leaders, and keep itself clean from sin.
MEMORY VERSE: Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses. —1 Timothy 5:19
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Acts 6:1-7 Support of the widows.
Tue.—Romans 12 Living in the body of Christ.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 9:1-15 Support of ministers.
Thu.—2 Corinthians 6 Faithful workers.
Fri.—Titus 3 Living as Christians
Devotional Reading: Hebrews 13 Christian Obligations.
Qualifications of Accepted Widows

1 Timothy 5:9-10 Let not a widow be taken into the number—It is evident here and in following verses that support of needy widows is meant. The qualifications set for them are: (1) At least threescore years old— an age of settled character. (2) Having been the wife of one man—one at a time, true to a husband all of his life. Second marriage after the death of a husband is not prohibited here, being consistent with 1 Timothy 5:14 and Romans 7:3. (3) Having a record of good works—Christian deeds. (4) Have brought up children—not necessarily children born to her, and been a good mother to teach and train them for God. I have known a number of saintly women who did much to raise children for God who never bore children of their own. (5) Have lodged strangers—used hospitality (Hebrews 13:1-2). In times and places where public accommodations are scanty, this virtue is very necessary. (6) Have washed the saints' feet—participated in the ordinance Jesus established. This includes also a life filled with the deeds of loving kindness and humility which the ordinance symbolizes (Colossians 3:12-14). (7) Have relieved the afflicted—given help to the sick, poor, friendless, discouraged, or any needy. (8) Diligently followed every good work—this supplies everything remaining for well-rounded Christian practice. Such are the widows to be provided for by the church.
Widows to Be Rejected

1 Timothy 5:11-16 Some widows were not to be accepted on this list. Younger widows refuse. Why? Because, being young, they would desire to remarry and fail to marry in the Lord, as the Bible instructs (1 Corinthians 7:39) and thus turn from the obligations of this special position. They would wax wanton against Christ—throw off the restraints, literally live as they please. Having damnation—not that of hell, but blame

SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 10

and condemnation for having backslid from their commitment. They cast off their first faith or promise. They would learn to be: (1) Idle—being supported by the church, they would feel no need to work. (2) Wandering about—not keepers at home (Titus 2:5). (3) Tattlers—telling to all what they heard from house to house (Proverbs 18:8). (4) Busybodies—meddling, always managing the business of others but never their own. (5) Speaking things which they ought not—all kinds of evil words. Idle words are bound to bring in some evil. What a charge to young widows! But Paul spoke from what he had seen—some are already turned aside from duties in the church after Satan. He advises these widows to marry the second time, bear children, guide the house, and thus avoid just blame.
Duties of Elders

1 Timothy 5:17-18 Support—elders that rule well . . . especially they who labor in the word and doctrine. Those who care well for the spiritual needs of the flock and teach, explain, preach, and apply God's Word are to receive double honor—due respect and greater financial reward. Their work requires more care and expense than does one that holds a lesser position. Paul quotes Scripture as authority in 1 Corinthians 9:7-14 and Luke 10:7.

1 Timothy 5:19-20 Accusations—Against an elder receive not an accusation. He who assumes any service of leadership invites criticism of it. An elder must at times use corrective measures which may arouse resentment. No accusation must be received unless fully proved by two or three witnesses. If proved, the offender must be rebuked before all to keep the church clear of approving and fostering sin.
Elders' Duties Concerning Individuals

Partiality—So prone are we to let our human feelings guide our actions in spiritual work that Paul reminds Timothy that the Father, the Son and the elect angels are seeing his actions. He charged him to use no partiality, not to prefer one more than another, either in support given, in rebuke of sin, or in favors shown. God is no respecter of persons; neither should we be.

1 Timothy 5:22-25 Sudden approval—God ordains elders, or chooses and places them (1 Corinthians 12:18). Then by prayer and laying on of hands, Christian leaders formally acknowledge God's ordination (1 Timothy 4:14). This must not be done suddenly—not without knowledge of the man's qualifications and call nor until he has proven himself worthy (1 Timothy 3:6-10). To do so would be taking part in the sin of putting an unfit man into sacred office and also to being a part of any harm he might do there. Keep thyself pure—free from any action of defiling the Church of God with unholy hands and uncalled leaders. Also, here lays the responsibility to preach and live the truth before all men. Either the sins or the good works of some candidates are open beforehand—easily seen. Those of others follow after—are seen only after careful investigation. Drink no longer water— alone—but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake . . . Timothy's health was necessary to keep him serving the church as an elder. The water was very unsuitable for drinking, and Paul found it necessary to remind Timothy to add a little juice from the fruit of the vine to make the water healthier for his body. Paul did not advocate the drinking of intoxicants. This would be unthinkable. Read Paul's writings in Ephesians 5:18 and 1 Corinthians 6:10.
JUST A THOUGHT
The drinking man commits suicide on the installment plan.

lessons.title: CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS IN THE CHURCH

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 11
FALSE RICHES
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 6:3-10

Is one right in believing that health and wealth compose Christianity? When you drive through a community and see well kept houses and big, well filled barns, is that Christianity? Is it right or wrong to have good things and a prosperous business? In what does the right or wrong lie? In the love of money, lies the wrong. The right attitude toward possessions, money, and necessary provisions is the difference between them being a blessing or a curse. Material riches are temporary. To love them is sin.

This lesson begins with two classes of people and traces their lives from the beginnings down through to their different ends. In these verses, main attention is given to the evil. The next lesson considers the righteous.
MEMORY VERSE: And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.—1 Timothy 6:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Deuteronomy 8:10-20 The giver of riches.
Tue.—2 Kings 5:20-27 Punishment for covetousness.
Wed.—Ecclesiastes 5:9-16 Money does not satisfy.
Thu.—Matthew 19:16-29 Possessions can be a hindrance.
Fri.—Luke 12:13-21 A rich fool.
Devotional Reading: James 5:1-9 Moth-eaten garments.
Christ's Way Versus the World's Way

1 Timothy 6:3-5 If any man teach otherwise—other than Paul had just outlined in the previous verses. Paul taught the Words of Christ and said (verse 2), These things teach and exhort. Paul urged in similar words a number of times through this Book. But some—sinners—would not consent or agree with Christ's Words, with doctrine . . . according to godliness. Those people, because they started off from the wrong foundation (their own human thoughts) and set before them the wrong principle, are filled with all kinds of evil—pride, ignorance, love of arguing over questions about the Word, twisting meanings and splitting hairs, name-calling and suspicion. Their minds are corrupt and filled with evil thoughts. Not taking the way of love, refusing the truth, they envy and fight and dispute. They reject the principle of godliness and take that of gain—thinking gain is godliness. They seek money and earthly possessions instead of things of God. Paul said, from such withdraw thyself.
Godliness and Contentment

1 Timothy 6:6-8 The natural, unsaved, worldly man lives by the false principle that gain is godliness, but Paul says the exact opposite is true—godliness . . . is great gain. Riches do not make one good, but godliness does make one rich in a better way. Godliness with contentment—because one has the godliness he most desires, he is contented with whatever he has of less value. Material comforts and possessions last only for this life. We do not bring them in with us, and we cannot take them out with us. If we have food and raiment— clothing and shelter—it is enough. Temporary things do only for a temporary life. For the eternal life of the soul,
