SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 11

better and lasting things are needed. It requires but little of this world's goods to satisfy a person who realizes he is not a citizen of this world, but of Heaven. Truly rich is the one who has godliness in his soul, food on his table, raiment and shelter for his body, and desires nothing more.
Covetousness Is the Way Down

1 Timothy 6:9-10 There is a very different result for those that will be rich. This desire is covetousness, the wish to get and to have, not to give, but to keep. One filled with this desire falls. The way is down, down, down. First, into temptation—they are tempted to selfishness, pride, stinginess, dishonesty, lying, etc. Further down into a snare—a trap with which Satan deceives and binds one in habits he never intended to practice. Down into lusts where chains of Satan are bound tighter and tighter. Foolish lusts which bring no lasting good, no spiritual blessing, and no soul-satisfaction. Hurtful lusts which lead to sins listed in preceding verses, make the heart hard, unloving, and selfish, and shut out God's voice. Finally, these lusts drown men in destruction—cut the line of communication with God and destroy their souls—and perdition—hereafter cast them into hell forever. Not much gain on this downward road, is there? For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? (Mark 8:36). The love of money—not money, which can do much good, but the love of it in the heart—is the root of all evil, or all kinds of evil, as were named. Coveting it causes one to err from the faith—to miss the mark—and to pierce oneself through with many sorrows. Such is the end of those who set gain rather than godliness and things more than God as their goal in life. Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death (Proverbs 11:4).
The Deceitfulness of Riches

Does it seem that our text is too severe with a lot of nice people? People who dress well, eat well, live in luxury are generally respected. To gain these and money besides seems to most to be a praiseworthy goal. Worldly riches deceive souls and cause them to feel that they are rich when they are truly poor. This goal is not enough. That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15). Often the rich are looked up to rather than the godly person. Why? Because there is a deception in worldly riches.

A story is told of a certain man who died. His obituary stated that "his chief ambition had been to own his own home, and he realized his ambition." Yet, even as that was being written, he lay dead. The earthly home was no longer his, and he had no greater ambition. Still, people said he had done well. Were they deceived? Was he? Are you deceived, dear one?
JUST A THOUGHT
Don't expect a bargain when you are shopping for sinful pursuits.

narrationUnits.text: Is one right in believing that health and wealth compose Christianity?
When you drive through a community and see well kept houses and big, well filled barns, is that Christianity?
Is it right or wrong to have good things and a prosperous business?
In what does the right or wrong lie?
In the love of money, lies the wrong.
The right attitude toward possessions, money, and necessary provisions is the difference between them being a blessing or a curse.
Material riches are temporary.
To love them is sin.
This lesson begins with two classes of people and traces their lives from the beginnings down through to their different ends.
In these verses, main attention is given to the evil.
The next lesson considers the righteous.
1 Timothy 6:3-5 If any man teach otherwise—other than Paul had just outlined in the previous verses.
Paul taught the Words of Christ and said (verse 2), These things teach and exhort.
Paul urged in similar words a number of times through this Book.
But some—sinners—would not consent or agree with Christ's Words, with doctrine . . . according to godliness.

Those people, because they started off from the wrong foundation (their own human thoughts) and set before them the wrong principle, are filled with all kinds of evil—pride, ignorance, love of arguing over questions about the Word, twisting meanings and splitting hairs, name-calling and suspicion.
Their minds are corrupt and filled with evil thoughts.
Not taking the way of love, refusing the truth, they envy and fight and dispute.
They reject the principle of godliness and take that of gain—thinking gain is godliness.
They seek money and earthly possessions instead of things of God.
Paul said, from such withdraw thyself.
1 Timothy 6:6-8 The natural, unsaved, worldly man lives by the false principle that gain is godliness, but Paul says the exact opposite is true—godliness . . . is great gain.
Riches do not make one good, but godliness does make one rich in a better way.
Godliness with contentment—because one has the godliness he most desires, he is contented with whatever he has of less value.
Material comforts and possessions last only for this life.
We do not bring them in with us, and we cannot take them out with us.
If we have food and raiment— clothing and shelter—it is enough.
Temporary things do only for a temporary life.
For the eternal life of the soul, better and lasting things are needed.
It requires but little of this world's goods to satisfy a person who realizes he is not a citizen of this world, but of Heaven.
Truly rich is the one who has godliness in his soul, food on his table, raiment and shelter for his body, and desires nothing more.

This desire is covetousness, the wish to get and to have, not to give, but to keep.
One filled with this desire falls.
The way is down, down, down.
First, into temptation—they are tempted to selfishness, pride, stinginess, dishonesty, lying, etc.
Further down into a snare—a trap with which Satan deceives and binds one in habits he never intended to practice.
Down into lusts where chains of Satan are bound tighter and tighter.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 12
TRUE RICHES
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 6:11-21

The rich are to use their riches in good works that they may lay hold on eternal life. Will these works save? No. Does each good deed add merit to one's account to be applied against one's sins, as some teach? No. Not by works of righteousness which we have done (Titus 3:5). No, works cannot save. We are saved by the riches of Christ's goodness, God's grace (Romans 2:4; Ephesians 1:7). We have redemption through the blood of Christ (Colossians 1:14). Where then do works find a place? They are an expression of faith. Faith without works is dead. Works indicate the quality of one's inner life. Every man will be judged according to his works. God sees both heart and deed. We can have true riches without a dime in our pocket. Read 2 Corinthians 6:10.
To know and obey God is true riches both in this life and in the one to come.
MEMORY VERSE: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not high minded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy. —1 Timothy 6:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Psalm 92 The blessing of the Lord.
Tue.—Luke 12:31-40 Treasure in the Heavens.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 8:1-15 A church rich in giving.
Thu.—Philippians 4:6-19 Looking to God to supply needs.
Fri.—Revelation 3:14-22 Gold tried in the fire.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 6:19-34 Incorruptible treasures.
The Right Way to Go

1 Timothy 6:11 Flee these things; and follow after. Here are two ways to go. Here are the same two lines of doctrine we studied in the last lesson—one, the Words of our Lord Jesus and the other, human ideas, or one, the way of righteousness, godliness, faith . . . and the other, the way of sin. Now, Paul says, flee one of these and follow after the other. Flee, run for your life, from the love of money and the many sins that go with it. This sin, the will to be rich, to gain the things of this world, is a strong and widespread temptation. Preacher and people alike are subject to it. Flee it; it is a matter of life or death. Money, of course, cannot bring satisfaction to the soul. Now the consideration turns to the right way, the way of Christ. Pursue it with your heart, soul, mind, and strength. Follow righteousness—obey the Lord from the heart, love His commandments, hate sin. Godliness—be like God, be holy, let Christ live in you. Faith—believe God, keep the channel of communication open between you and God. Love—have the love of God in the heart, exercise that love, love God and men. Patience—endure calmly and faithfully any work, hardship, misunderstanding, or persecution. Meekness —be gentle, consider others ahead of yourself, and be submissive to God and to right in everything.
Fight the Good Fight

1 Timothy 6:12 Fight—Timothy was fighting with Satan to gain eternal life. He had already been a witness to the truth of the Gospel and to his own faithfulness to it before many witnesses. The way of Christ was a much persecuted way there. Christians professed Christ at risk of losing all they possessed, even their lives. Timothy had suffered persecution and imprisonment and held true (Hebrews 13:23). Timothy fought

LESSON 12

against persecutors as well as spirits. Today our greatest battle is against deceiving spirits (Ephesians 6:11-12), spirits which lead us to believe we are right when we are wrong, that we can do wrong and get by. Our battle is truly a daily fight of faith—our faith in God. Lay hold on eternal life—a better prize than earthly contests can ever offer. The prize can be gained. Read 2 Timothy 4:6-7.
A Solemn Charge

1 Timothy 6:13-16 Here Paul lays a solemn charge on Timothy—binds him under obligation. He calls God and Christ as witnesses, reminding Timothy that they see how he fulfills his duty. God, who quickeneth—He has the power of life. Christ endured His suffering and death without sin and convinced Pilate of His righteousness. Timothy was told what to do and the purpose of it. Keep this commandment—this Gospel— without spot. Pass it on pure and unchanged. Unrebukeable—obey it so fully that no guilt can be found in him. How long? This Gospel and this record are to be kept for all generations until Jesus comes again. The purpose is to be ready for His coming. In his times he shall shew—or He will appear at the appointed time, which no man knows (Mark 13:32). Who is He? Our Lord Jesus Christ. In the description that follows is the greatest exaltation that human language can voice. Can any read it and doubt that Jesus is God? He is blessed—favored of God; only Potentate— only ruler with all power and authority; the King above all kings; Lord above all lords; only One with immortality—with inherent eternal life, Who cannot die; dwelling in the light which no man can approach—a glory far beyond man's comprehension; no man . . . can see—finite man is incapable of seeing infinite God (John 1:18). Jacob and Moses saw a manifestation of God in Genesis 32:30 and Exodus 33:11. This greatest, highest One will have honor and power everlasting—forever and ever.
The Right Use of Riches

1 Timothy 6:17-19 Some people are rich in this world. Having wealth is not sin. Loving it, trusting in it, using it selfishly is. Timothy was to charge the rich—by teaching them their responsible duty. What was he to tell them? (1) Be not high-minded—not proud, overbearing, for riches do not make one better. (2) Do not trust in uncertain riches—they can do nothing spiritually for us; they can soon vanish. (3) Trust in God—He lives, He gives us all things, can give all spiritual blessings. (4) Do good, that they be rich in good works. What works? To distribute, to communicate. This is to give to those who need, and to give for the spread of the Gospel. Thus they lay up in store true riches (Matthew 6:19-21). These are a good foundation for the time to come—the Judgment and the next or heavenly dispensation. This record will please God and help to obtain the greatest riches, eternal life.
Paul's Plea to Timothy

1 Timothy 6:20-21 O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust. What was committed to Timothy? The Gospel, both to keep in his own heart and pass on to others by use of the spiritual gifts he had received. Timothy was in danger of losing it. Everyone is in this danger as long as we are in the world in reach of Satan's temptations. What might steal his faith? Profane and vain babblings—earthly, human ideas of those who know nothing of the spiritual things of God. Oppositions of science falsely so called—not true science, but philosophies that oppose the truth of God. Some professing—adopting these false ideas— have erred—have turned from the faith, from the truth of the Gospel. But Timothy, avoid these things. Grace be with thee—the life of God in you to keep you from the wrong and to keep you in the truth.

We are saved by the riches of Christ's goodness, God's grace (Romans 2:4; Ephesians 1:7).
We have redemption through the blood of Christ (Colossians 1:14).
Where then do works find a place?
They are an expression of faith.
Faith without works is dead.
Works indicate the quality of one's inner life.
Every man will be judged according to his works.
God sees both heart and deed.
We can have true riches without a dime in our pocket.
Read 2 Corinthians 6:10.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 6:11 Flee these things; and follow after. Here are two ways to go. Here are the same two lines of doctrine we studied in the last lesson—one, the Words of our Lord Jesus and the other, human ideas, or one, the way of righteousness, godliness, faith . . . and the other, the way of sin. Now, Paul says, flee one of these and follow after the other. Flee, run for your life, from the love of money and the many sins that go with it. This sin, the will to be rich, to gain the things of this world, is a strong and widespread temptation. Preacher and people alike are subject to it. Flee it; it is a matter of life or death. Money, of course, cannot bring satisfaction to the soul. Now the consideration turns to the right way, the way of Christ. Pursue it with your heart, soul, mind, and strength. Follow righteousness—obey the Lord from the heart, love His commandments, hate sin. Godliness—be like God, be holy, let Christ live in you. Faith—believe God, keep the channel of communication open between you and God. Love—have the love of God in the heart, exercise that love, love God and men. Patience—endure calmly and faithfully any work, hardship, misunderstanding, or persecution. Meekness —be gentle, consider others ahead of yourself, and be submissive to God and to right in everything.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 6:12 Fight—Timothy was fighting with Satan to gain eternal life. He had already been a witness to the truth of the Gospel and to his own faithfulness to it before many witnesses. The way of Christ was a much persecuted way there. Christians professed Christ at risk of losing all they possessed, even their lives. Timothy had suffered persecution and imprisonment and held true (Hebrews 13:23). Timothy fought against persecutors as well as spirits. Today our greatest battle is against deceiving spirits (Ephesians 6:11-12), spirits which lead us to believe we are right when we are wrong, that we can do wrong and get by. Our battle is truly a daily fight of faith—our faith in God. Lay hold on eternal life—a better prize than earthly contests can ever offer. The prize can be gained. Read 2 Timothy 4:6-7.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 6:13-16 Here Paul lays a solemn charge on Timothy—binds him under obligation. He calls God and Christ as witnesses, reminding Timothy that they see how he fulfills his duty. God, who quickeneth—He has the power of life. Christ endured His suffering and death without sin and convinced Pilate of His righteousness. Timothy was told what to do and the purpose of it. Keep this commandment—this Gospel— without spot. Pass it on pure and unchanged. Unrebukeable—obey it so fully that no guilt can be found in him. How long? This Gospel and this record are to be kept for all generations until Jesus comes again. The purpose is to be ready for His coming. In his times he shall shew—or He will appear at the appointed time, which no man knows (Mark 13:32). Who is He? Our Lord Jesus Christ. In the description that follows is the greatest exaltation that human language can voice. Can any read it and doubt that Jesus is God? He is blessed—favored of God; only Potentate— only ruler with all power and authority; the King above all kings; Lord above all lords; only One with immortality—with inherent eternal life, Who cannot die; dwelling in the light which no man can approach—a glory far beyond man's comprehension; no man . . . can see—finite man is incapable of seeing infinite God (John 1:18). Jacob and Moses saw a manifestation of God in Genesis 32:30 and Exodus 33:11. This greatest, highest One will have honor and power everlasting—forever and ever.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 6:17-19 Some people are rich in this world. Having wealth is not sin. Loving it, trusting in it, using it selfishly is. Timothy was to charge the rich—by teaching them their responsible duty. What was he to tell them? (1) Be not high-minded—not proud, overbearing, for riches do not make one better. (2) Do not trust in uncertain riches—they can do nothing spiritually for us; they can soon vanish. (3) Trust in God—He lives, He gives us all things, can give all spiritual blessings. (4) Do good, that they be rich in good works. What works? To distribute, to communicate. This is to give to those who need, and to give for the spread of the Gospel. Thus they lay up in store true riches (Matthew 6:19-21). These are a good foundation for the time to come—the Judgment and the next or heavenly dispensation. This record will please God and help to obtain the greatest riches, eternal life.

paragraphs.text: 1 Timothy 6:20-21 O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust. What was committed to Timothy? The Gospel, both to keep in his own heart and pass on to others by use of the spiritual gifts he had received. Timothy was in danger of losing it. Everyone is in this danger as long as we are in the world in reach of Satan's temptations. What might steal his faith? Profane and vain babblings—earthly, human ideas of those who know nothing of the spiritual things of God. Oppositions of science falsely so called—not true science, but philosophies that oppose the truth of God. Some professing—adopting these false ideas— have erred—have turned from the faith, from the truth of the Gospel. But Timothy, avoid these things. Grace be with thee—the life of God in you to keep you from the wrong and to keep you in the truth.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 13
RICHES—FORTUNE OR MISFORTUNE?
Scripture Text: Mark 10:17-31

We have studied Paul's teaching concerning true and false riches. In this lesson we take notice of one portion of Scripture in which Jesus deals with this subject. Jesus spoke of riches in many places throughout the New Testament. He considered it very important in the Christian's progress. He taught that to obtain eternal life is the greatest pursuit. Love of material possessions shuts out one from God. Not only must our actions be right, but our hearts must be changed. God rewards both here and hereafter for everything left behind for His sake. True disciples of Christ will be persecuted.
MEMORY VERSE: How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!—Mark 10:23b
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Deuteronomy 8:10-18 Gratitude for riches.
Tue.—James 1:9-11; James 5:1-9 Vanity of riches.
Wed.—1 Timothy 6:7-12, 1 Timothy 6:17-19 Advice to the rich.
Thu.—Romans 12:1-8 Giving selves to the Lord.
Fri.—Philippians 3:4-11 Paul's denial of self for Christ.
Devotional Reading: Isaiah 55 The great invitation.
Seek Eternal Life

Mark 10:17-18 Jesus and His disciples walked toward Jerusalem where He would be put to death. There came one running, and kneeled to him. His running indicates determined urgency to overtake Jesus before He was gone. Kneeling indicates respect and humility. He was seeking the best gift man can attain—eternal life. Matthew's account (Matthew 19:16) tells us that he asked, What good thing shall I do ... ? The way to God is not by good works or accomplishments or sufferings. No! Believing rather than doing opens the way to God. The heart must be changed. This man (Matthew tells us he was young and Luke that he was a ruler) called Jesus, Good Master. Jesus answered, Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is God. The thing that made Jesus good was the only thing that makes any other person good, a work of God's goodness in the heart, making one a son of God.

When the Bible speaks of eternal life, it means not only its quantity—endless—but also its quality— heavenly. It is that life which God has. It is the life that is in His Son Jesus (1 John 5:11-12). It is the life that He gives to His people (Galatians 2:20). It is holy and ever growing. It cannot cease to be, but it can depart from us if we let sin in. It is the greatest treasure. Seek it above all else.
Jesus Tells the Way

Mark 10:19-21 Jesus first pointed him to the Law given through Moses. Keeping it is not enough to save one (Romans 3:28; Romans 8:3), and Jesus wanted the man to realize this from his own experience of trying to keep it and yet remaining unsatisfied and without eternal life. Jesus beholding him loved him—because He loved him, He told him the truth of his condition. One thing thou lackest—he had not left all, he did not love God with all his heart, soul, mind, and strength. He still loved himself and the world. Go ... sell ... and give ... and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take ... and follow me. To supply his lack, he must fully

LESSON 13
surrender, be willing to sell all, give away the proceeds, take the way of sacrifice, and follow Jesus. He would have far greater treasure than before (Matthew 6:19-20; Mark 8:34-36).
Riches a Hindrance

Mark 10:22-27 The young man made a wrong decision. He went away grieved—offended by the Words of Jesus. He went away from Jesus, peace, joy, a life of service to Christ, and endless bliss in Heaven with God. He went to sadness, grief, remorse, despair, darkness, and death. In just a short time, he lost his riches to the Roman Army in their devastation of Jerusalem. How hard is it ... What a hold possessions can have upon one! They have an intoxicating charm that drives one to get more and more. It is not only those that have money who love it. Some of the poorest people are bound by the power of the love of riches. We call riches a fortune. In the light of the Bible, would they better be called a misfortune? The disciples were astonished at Jesus' Words! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle ... He compared it to a rich man entering the kingdom. It is impossible with men. Jesus said it plainly. Only God can cleanse the love and trust of money from a rich man's heart and fit him into the kingdom.
The Reward for Dedication

Mark 10:28-31 Jesus had promised the young man treasure in heaven if he obeyed. Peter was reminded of his experience. What would the disciples have for giving up all for Jesus? An hundredfold now and eternal life hereafter. For giving up family, the dedicated one has loving spiritual brothers and sisters. For giving up possessions, he has his needs supplied by God through His people. The joy from these and in the world to come is immeasurable riches. But with persecutions. Satan and the world always oppose those who go all the way with Jesus. First shall be last ... Jesus explains His meaning of this verse in the parable of Matthew 20:1-16. Equal riches are for all who qualify.
The Consecrated Life

We may hold in our possession many things—material, physical, mental, and spiritual. To follow Christ, some of these must be sacrificed, others dedicated. Anything that would hinder the full life of Christ in us must be left, cast aside, sacrificed. Those things that can be used in His service must be presented to Him, fully yielded, dedicated. We must dedicate ourselves to use them at His Holy Spirit's direction. The child of God consecrates his possessions, hands, tongue, mind, abilities, and all for God's use.

Since money can become so destructive to character, if used without reference to Christian ideals, it becomes very important that every Christian be well acquainted with the Gospel teachings on this matter. The Christian life involves Christian stewardship. No matter how prominent we may appear in the picture, we must realize that everything we have has been given to us either directly or indirectly by God. One must make a friend of money and thus keep money from becoming his enemy. He must recognize money as a servant and never allow it to become his master. Here is a great truth—we get out of life what we put into it. For God loveth a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7b).
JUST A THOUGHT
The spirit in which we give is more important than the gift itself.

The Christian life involves Christian stewardship. No matter how prominent we may appear in the picture, we must realize that everything we have has been given to us either directly or indirectly by God. One must make a friend of money and thus keep money from becoming his enemy. He must recognize money as a servant and never allow it to become his master. Here is a great truth—we get out of life what we put into it. For God loveth a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7b).

lines.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 1
HOLD TO SOUND DOCTRINE
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 1:1-20
This quarter we study into the close association of Paul
and Timothy, a relationship which was never broken.
The Book of First Timothy was written by Paul to
Timothy, a young minister of the Gospel of Christ. Paul wrote the letter for the purpose that Timothy would be
encouraged and strengthened in holding to the sound doctrine of Christ as he had taught him. Paul, in stirring the
spirit of Timothy, lays before each follower of Christ the truth that the work of the church must be done through
the gifts of the Spirit. Leaders must be called of God and be examples of godly living.
Timothy had been called to the work of the ministry and had been given the necessary gift of the Spirit by
which to carry it on. Paul's confidence in him was not disappointed. His letters to Timothy show affection,
esteem, and trust. To the Philippians, he said of him, I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for
your state (Philippians 2:19-23). We must hold fast to the truth of Christ and refuse false teachings.
MEMORY VERSE: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.—3 John 4
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Isaiah 55 Promise of salvation.
Tue.—John 6:26-51 Doctrine of Jesus.
Wed.—Hebrews 6:1-8 Danger of falling.
Thu.—Hebrews 12:1-15 Steadfastness.
Fri.—2 John Abiding in the truth.
Devotional Reading: Colossians 2 —Be established in the truth.
The Relationship of Saints
1 Timothy 1:1-2 In the warm greeting of Paul to Timothy which opens this letter, we see that each occupied
a genuine abiding place in the church, the body of Christ—Paul was an apostle of Jesus Christ, Timothy, my
own son in the faith. Each entered his position by the spiritual act of God—Paul, by the commandment of
God, Timothy, a son in the faith. And they were bound together in a close fellowship of love. These three
characteristics are present in the Church of God.
The relationship of saints one to another is spiritual, and it is real. It is the closest union humans have with
each other. Saints are related by the blood of Christ, born of the same Father, possessed of the same Spirit. They
are branches growing on the same Vine. The world knows nothing of such. Clubs and so-called churches may
have a business and social relationship, but no kinship, no spiritual fellowship, and no joy in one another such as
the church has.
1 Timothy 1:3-4 Paul left Timothy at Ephesus while he went on to Macedonia. The Ephesian church was
slipping from the state of purity they had when Paul wrote of his thankfulness for their faith and love and said
they trusted in Christ and were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise (Ephesians 1:12-16). They had
begun to leave their first love, a state described by Christ in Revelation 2:1-7. False teachers and bad examples
were among them. Timothy must teach them to hold to true doctrine. Some evils which had crept in were
fables—groundless legends, traditions, and opinions and genealogies—tracings of ancestry back to Abraham
and tribal leaders. These had no basis in Scripture or authority from God. Such minister questions—raise
disputes, doubts, separations over opinions. The opposite of this is godly edifying which is in faith. Progress in
godliness can come only by way of faith—believing in God's Word and obeying it.

LESSON 1
A Program of Love
1 Timothy 1:5-10 Paul pointed Timothy to the end of the commandment—the goal of God's dealings with
man. The purpose of God's relation to man shown in the Law and the Prophets and completed in the atoning
work of Christ is charity—the love of God filling the heart of man. God IS love. This love radiates out. It comes
out of a pure heart. Love comes out of a good conscience, made good when sin is forgiven. It comes out of
faith unfeigned—unpretended, genuine—for faith is necessary to receive God or any of His gifts. Thus faith, a
clear conscience, and a pure heart are steps to reaching the experience God plans for us. Some have missed it
because they have turned aside unto vain jangling—useless words, arguing, contention, trying to teach things
they do not understand. Paul names things that are contrary to sound doctrine in verses 8-11.
Paul's Testimony
1 Timothy 1:11-17 Being reminded of the glorious Gospel, Paul begins to testify of what that Gospel has
meant to his life. (1) It was Christ, not Paul himself, who put him into his place of service. God filled him with
faith and love, that which is in Christ Jesus. (2) Paul tells of his former life while in sin—blasphemer . . .
persecutor . . . injurious. Paul owned to being the chief of sinners. (3) Paul obtained mercy, because he did it
ignorantly. He thought he was doing right (Acts 26:9). As soon as Paul knew the truth, he obeyed it (Acts
26:19). (4) Christ's mission to the world was to save sinners. (5) Paul obtained mercy so that Christ might
shew forth all longsuffering—might demonstrate His saving work—for a pattern, or example, to them which
should hereafter believe on him—on Christ—to life everlasting. (6) Then Paul breaks forth in thanks and
praise to the God Who had done all this. He calls Him King eternal—Ruler of all forever; immortal—
deathless, incorruptible; invisible—not seen, yet He is strongly felt in His works; only wise God—none beside
Him. Paul gave Him honor and glory forever and ever— endlessly.
A Charge to Timothy
1 Timothy 1:18-20 This charge I commit unto thee—the work for which Paul left Timothy in Ephesus, to
teach the church to hold to true doctrine and avoid false teachings. Timothy was to carry it on according to the
prophecies—according to the spiritual gift and the instructions for its use which God gave him (1 Timothy
4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6-9). Prophecies are Words from God. Timothy was to war a good warfare. He was to hold
faith, and a good conscience. Others, neglecting to do so, made shipwreck of their souls. Two names of
individuals who had done so are named here. The delivering unto Satan is a punishment for blasphemy against
the leading of the Holy Spirit in their lives. That they may learn. What a tragic lesson! Are we treating sin too
lightly when we think we can have forgiveness whenever we ask it, regardless of our previous knowledge?
JUST A THOUGHT
A lame man on the right road will beat a fast man on the wrong road.

LESSON 2
PAUL TEACHES PRAYER HABITS
Scripture Text: 1Timothy 2:1-8
Paul wrote to pass on to Timothy what the Holy Spirit and experience had
taught him of what a minister should be and of what the church should be. He urged
Timothy to be always loyal to the doctrine of Christ, faithful to the call of God, and
to pray much. He was to lead and teach the church as God led him. Prayer had a very important place in this. All
saints should pray for all people from pure, holy hearts.
The church needed these teachings in all of its history, but, perhaps, never more than now. Present decay of
moral standards, lukewarmness, and paganism in much of the religious world and the increasing encroachment
by evil forces point up our need for the admonitions of Paul. As we study 1 Timothy, we will find many
subjects of vital importance to the church today.
MEMORY VERSE: The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.—James 5:16b
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Judges 6:36-40 Seeking God's will.
Tue.—2 Kings 20:1-11 Hezekiah’s prayer.
Wed.—Psalm 5 A prayer of David.
Thu.—Daniel 9:1-22 Daniel’s prayer of confession.
Fri.—Matthew 7:7-11; John 16:23-27 God's prayer promise.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 6:5-15 Manner of praying.
Pray for All Men
1 Timothy 2:1-4 I exhort therefore—therefore always refers back to something before as the reason for
making the present statement. Just before, Paul had urged Timothy to hold true to the faith of Christ. Some had
made shipwreck by putting away this faith. For one way to avoid such disaster, Paul exhorted to prayer first of
all—most important. Supplications—prayers for protection from evils or removal of troubles. Prayers—asking
for the supply of one's own needs, spiritual or material. Intercessions—asking for the supply of needs of others.
Giving of thanks—thanksgiving and praise to God for all that He is and all that He does for us and for others.
These cover all the phases of Christian prayer. Prayer should be made for all men.
For kings, and for all that are in authority—All of us are dependent upon government. We should ask
God to guide rulers and leaders, give them wisdom, incline their hearts and minds toward Him, prosper their
good acts, and guard them from wrong ones. The granting of such prayers will produce better conditions in our
world. Praying for all men and for rulers is good and acceptable in the sight of God. Surely, saints will do it,
for they want, above all, to please God as well as to gain the other benefits. God wants these prayers because He
desires all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. Prayers of the saints are
cooperation with God. Their prayers can actually influence the quality of government.
One Universal Remedy
1 Timothy 2:5-6 One mediator Who is a ransom for all—ONLY one, but enough to save EVERY person.
A mediator makes peace between, and joins together. Sin separates God and man. Jesus gave himself a ransom
on the Cross to take away the enmity, the sins, and join God and the cleansed sinner together as Father and son
© 2015 Church of God, Inc.
Paul Teaches Prayer Habits─ Lesson 2
www.GodsAcres.org
SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 2
or daughter. God wills that all be saved. He makes the way for all to be saved. This is the reason for our praying
for all men. Praying releases the power of God to save souls and to work all kinds of good.
Christ gave Himself a ransom to be testified—witnessed— in due time. Since the gift is for all, all must be
told. (See Acts 1:8.) This is the basis for all Christian work. We read in Proverbs 11:30 that he that wins souls
is wise. This wisdom comes by prayer.
Paul's Place in the Church
1 Timothy 2:7 Paul was one witness. Whereunto—to the task of carrying the news of Christ's atonement to
all—I am ordained—set apart, chosen. God chose Paul as a preacher—a proclaimer— and an apostle—one
sent to new places with a message—a teacher of the Gentiles (Acts 9:15; Acts 26:16-18). Paul's message was
in faith and verity, or in Spirit and truth. It was not vague, no mere "social gospel" or moral and economic
uplift. It was of Jesus Christ, the one mediator and ransom for all. Paul was sure of his calling (I speak the truth
. . . lie not). God has a definite work for each one now (1 Corinthians 12:18).
Paul said, "I am ordained a preacher." This was not the formal ordination of a human committee or board
passing Paul's credentials and authorizing him to preach. It was not even the approval of his brethren and the
laying on of their hands. God chose Paul (Acts 9:15). He laid out the work he was to do. God made him a
minister and a witness. He enabled him to open the eyes of the Gentiles and turn them to God (Acts 26:16-18).
This was Paul's ordination. No one can serve acceptably with less.
How to Pray
1 Timothy 2:8 I will therefore . . . (1) that we may live peaceably and godly, (2) that all men be saved, and
(3) that all people be told of Christ's payment of ransom for them—that men pray everywhere. Not only in
church assemblies, but at all times and all places. Who can pray? Only those who do it acceptably to God.
Lifting up holy hands—free from sin. Iniquities separate between us and God (Isaiah 59:1-2). See also Psalm
24:3-4. Without wrath—God is love. The heart must be free from grudges, unforgiveness, or ill feeling against
another. And doubting—God's promises are to those who believe. Doubting and unbelief cut one off from His
blessings (James 1:6-7).
Timothy was instructed to lead the Ephesians into habits of prayer. They were to pray for the salvation of all
people through Christ. They were to pray in faith and love and holy living. They were to pray at all times and
places. These instructions apply to each of us.
Prayer is communication with God. The church cannot be healthy and prospering without continuing in this
Christian privilege. Four phases of prayer are named. None can be left out without harm to prayer and lack to
the praying ones. Bible reading aids prayer. How?
"When the glory of the Father is the goal of every prayer, When before the throne of Heaven our High Priest
presents them there; when the Spirit prompts the asking; when the pleading heart believes; then we know of
each petition everyone who asks receives."
JUST A THOUGHT
Some people pray for more things than they are willing to work for.

LESSON 3
THE CONDUCT OF WOMEN
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 2:9-15
When either women or men spend much time, cost, and attention on decorating themselves, they reveal that
they have a lack within and that they are trying to supply that lack by the aids of dress and adornment.
What effect does the dress of women have upon their spirituality? How does it affect others? What is the
best adornment? In what ways are the positions of men and women in the church equal? In what ways are they
different?
Paul, in today's lesson, gives answers to these questions and teaches that God is no respecter of persons—
male or female.
MEMORY VERSE: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing
of gold, or of putting on of apparel.—1 Peter 3:3
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—2 Kings 22 Huldah the prophetess.
Tue.—Luke 2:36-38; Acts 2:14-18; Acts 21:9 Women prophesied.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 14:1-6 Prophesying described.
Thu.—Galatians 3:26-29 All are one in Christ.
Fri.—1 Peter 3:1-9 Instructions to wives.
Devotional Reading: Proverbs 31:10-31 The virtuous woman.
Dress and Adornment
1 Timothy 2:9-10 In like manner also—like men were instructed in the preceding verse. They were
instructed to pray in holiness, love, and faith. Out of the same kind of saintly lives, women are to adorn
themselves. God loves beauty. Witness the exquisite and varied beauty He has lavished upon nature. To please
Him, it must be true beauty, must be spiritual beauty of the heart and soul, not outer veneer or artificial
decoration. See Isaiah 60:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:21. Paul speaks of the negative first. The adornment must not
be that of broided hair—hair braided and entwined with gold, silver, etc. Gold …pearls…costly array. These
are outward, material, perishable things. Instead, Paul turns to the positive side. Women must dress in modest
apparel—decent, chaste, reserved, not bold, inconspicuous dress that covers the body without calling undue
attention to either the person or the apparel. With shamefacedness—a desire to avoid anything alluring,
extreme, flashy, or immodest. Without pride. Modest women dislike calling attention to themselves. Sobriety—
with moderation, serious-mindedness, and simplicity. Clothing should not be extravagant either in expense or in
style. It should be becoming, neither slovenly nor showy. It should be worn as a covering, not as a means of
exciting admiration.
God desires His children to be adorned with good works. These add beauty to men and women professing
godliness. Good works outside are produced by a good spirit inside. God sees as an ornament of great price, a
meek and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:3-4). To His church, God says, Put on thy beautiful garments (Isaiah 52:1).
God not only tells us what adornment to leave off, but He tells us what to put on to please Him.
The Bible does not prescribe details of styles and materials of dress, but it does set standards by which we
can regulate our dress. It does not hold us to uniform attire. Dress can have much to do with feeding sinful pride.
Saints should not dress and allow their children to dress as the world in shorts, halters, bathing suits, etc. God
has but one standard for both.

The Conduct of Women─ Lesson 3
www.GodsAcres.org

LESSON 3
Woman's Place of Service
1 Timothy 2:11-12 Silence with all subjection. In what respect is this enjoined upon women? Paul makes it
more clearly in 1 Corinthians 14:34-35. Brethren are to take the lead; sisters are to follow. Both Jewish and
civil Roman law forbade women from doing what belonged especially to men. That women were acting in a
disrespectful manner seems evident—they were to be in subjection, not to usurp authority (to boss), to be
under obedience. Usurp means to take possession of without right or by force. Their speaking seems to have
been asking questions, disputing, and disrupting in public assemblies—if they will learn anything, let them
ask their husbands at home. Women had been held back and deprived of assembly gatherings; they did not
know how to conduct themselves. Paul was not saying that women could not preach or teach God's message. We
read in both the Old and New Testaments of women who prophesied. (See Daily Readings.) The Holy Spirit was
poured out upon both men and women. Read Acts 2:16-18; Joel 2:28-29. Prophesying by women appears to
have been common. Paul deals with it in 1 Corinthians 11:5. In Philippians 4:3 Paul speaks of those women
which labored with me in the gospel.
Would God have given to women the gift of prophecy or of teaching and the burden of using it and led them
into places of service if He did not will that they use it? What does it signify that all of the twelve Apostles and
authors of the Bible Books were men? In times past, most leadership was given to men, but women have been
called by God to preach too. The brethren in places of leadership will not impose unjust or painful restrictions
upon the sisters in Christ. Nor will the sisters, in exercising the gifts God has given them, depart from the
womanly character of modesty, meekness, and gentleness. A woman filling the place to which God has called
her is not usurping authority; that authority has been given to her rightfully. Neither men nor women should
attempt to choose their work without the call of God, but having been placed by Him (1 Corinthians 12:18),
each should fill that place as He leads.
The Influence of Eve
1 Timothy 2:13-15 Adam was first formed . . . was not deceived— was not the one misled by Satan into
sin. Eve was deceived into eating the forbidden fruit and first to sin (Genesis 2:18, 22; Genesis 3:6). These two
facts are given as the reason for the subjection of women to men. Does this subjection extend to the point
where women are denied salvation? No. She shall be saved in child-bearing. Does motherhood save one? No.
Only faith in Christ saves. "Saved in childbearing." Salvation came through a Child that was born because Jesus
was the seed of Eve (Genesis 3:15) and was born of a woman, Mary (Galatians 4:4-5). Jesus became the Savior
by Whom all must be saved, if at all, both men and women, for there is neither male nor female: for ye are all
one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). Women as well as men are saved if they continue in faith and charity
and holiness with sobriety. Jesus gave women freedom they had never known before.
JUST A THOUGHT
God is in the cleansing business not the white-washing business.

LESSON 4
CHARACTER OF A BISHOP
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 3:1-7
A bishop or elder must be a true Christian in every way— toward his
home, the church, and the world.
Are elders chosen or are they placed? Both. In all of God's work in the
world, there is an inner current between God and man, a mutual working, a
spiritual unity. God places certain abilities in a person. He has a desire to use
that ability for good. He yields his life to God. He prays for spiritual gifts,
always submissive to God's will. God gives; the man exercises and develops.
God calls and places. Just how He works it all, we cannot tell, but there is a
divine harmony in it which is beautiful to see. It brings true success in God's
work and joy to the worker (1 Corinthians 12:18).
MEMORY VERSE: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially they who
labor in the word and doctrine.—1 Timothy 5:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Ezekiel 33:1-16 Responsibility of a pastor.
Tue.—Acts 20:17-38 Paul counsels the elders.
Wed.—Ephesians 4:7-16 Gifts for perfecting the church.
Thu.—1 Thessalonians 2:1-12 In trust with the Gospel.
Fri.—1 Peter 5 An elder and his flock.
Devotional Reading: Titus 1:1-9 To ordain elders.
Desiring Spiritual Gifts
1 Timothy 3:1 If a man desire the office of a bishop— this is a rightful desire. Covet earnestly the best
gifts—gifts of the Spirit to fit one for service. Desire spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:31; 1 Corinthians 14:1).
Elder designates the rank or position. Originally meaning older, it is used to mean leading or superior. Bishop
and pastor denote the functions. Bishop means overseer or superintendent. Pastor means one who feeds the
flock, a shepherd. The same men are called elders and bishops in Titus 1:5, 7. Pastors are used in Ephesians
4:11. He desireth a good work. It is good to lead, teach, and bring to Christ, feed spiritually, protect, comfort,
encourage, and build up the flock of God. There is a great need for more to desire this work. It is good both in
what it accomplishes and in the rewards it brings to the doer. But every privilege brings its responsibilities.
Are all elders who are called elders? Many are trying to fill the position that are neither qualified nor called
of God. What is wrong? They were appointed or elected by man rather than by God. We cannot make one an
elder or bishop by electing him. God must both call and place him. We are told to desire, even covet, spiritual
gifts and office, preferring that of prophecy. Our Scripture lists the requirements for being a bishop or elder. For
clarity, let us number them in order and divide them according to the phase of life covered.
Personal Character
1 Timothy 3:2-3 (1) A bishop then must be blameless—a clear connection with God, justified, righteous,
holy, one against whom no blame can be rightly laid. (2) The husband of one wife— one at a time, not a
bigamist. An elder is not required to be married. Paul was not. However, he was not a settled pastor except for
limited times, rather an apostle and evangelist. Yet, does not Christian marriage make a good pastor a better one
© 2015 Church of God, Inc.
Character of a Bishop─ Lesson 4
www.GodsAcres.org
SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 4
by improving his effectiveness and providing him a help mate? (3) Vigilant—watchful, attentive to duty and to
the needs of the people. (4) Sober—of sound mind, wise in judgment, serious- minded, self-controlled. (5) Of
good behavior—of orderly, right, courteous, and refined conduct. Silliness, rudeness, and inconsiderateness
have no place in the work of God. (6) Given to hospitality—inclined to receive and entertain those away from
home or in need. See Hebrews 13:1-3. (7) Apt to teach— both able and willing to communicate his knowledge
to others, having clear understanding of the truths of God, and the ability to make them clear to others. He will
use his ability both in preaching and in teaching publicly and privately. This necessitates constant study and
prayer. He strives to master the Bible. (8) Not given to wine—a total abstainer from intoxicating beverages, and
also, from tobacco and drugs. (9) No striker— not disposed to defend himself or his doctrine by force, not
desiring to harm or destroy those who oppose him, no persecutor. (10) Patient—meeting suffering, hardness, or
injustices with calmness, persevering in right, letting love overrule. (11) Not a brawler—quiet, peaceable, not
contentious, not quarrelsome, not making noisy disturbance. (12) Not covetous—not desiring gain for himself,
not desiring the things of others. (13) Not greedy of filthy lucre—unselfish, not preaching for money, not
loving money for its own sake, no ill-gotten gains, not desiring money more than spiritual things.
Family Life
1 Timothy 3:4-5 (14) One that ruleth well his own house—takes the leadership of his family as a husband
and father should. He does it well, is neither a slave driver nor indifferent. Having his children in subjection—
requiring obedience from them, directing their actions, and knowing where they are and what they are doing. He
will teach his children to be good examples, polite, and respectful of others and not be unruly. (15) With all
gravity—with seriousness, thoughtfulness. He thinks of the children's needs physically, mentally, and
spiritually. Because he loves them, he is careful to do his best to supply them. This is required because his home
is a man's first responsibility, and if he know not how to rule his own house, neither can he care for the Church
of God. The ability required is the same for both.
Experience
1 Timothy 3:6 (16) Not a novice—not a beginner or newly converted or inexperienced. How can one who
does not yet know the way, lead others? How can one who has not yet learned, teach others? When he shows
himself worthy and has enough experience to walk ahead of his people, let him lead them. A novice raised to
leadership is in danger of the sin of pride, by which he will fall into the condemnation of the devil. Pride is a
weakness most easily fallen into.
Community Reputation
1 Timothy 3:7 (17) He must have a good report of them which are without—respected by the
unconverted world. Unsaved people will not feel fellowship with a saint will not understand or agree with him
and may not like him, but his life must be so upright that they will respect it and call it good. If it is otherwise,
he will bring reproach—shame—upon himself and the church, fail to lead people to Christ, and will be caught
in the snare of the devil—devil's trap. God does not have a double standard. The rules in our lesson for bishops
and elders are for the rest of the church also. The same standard of holiness and perfection is given to us all.
JUST A THOUGHT
To hear truth and refuse it does not nullify truth.

LESSON 5
CHARACTER OF A DEACON
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 3:8-15
What is the authority of a deacon? Is it to work independently of the
elder? Is it to hear from God and make clear His will to the people? Is it to
take the offering, serve the Lord's Supper, or paint the building? He
certainly has no authority in deciding matters such as calling a preacher or
an evangelist to hold meetings. An elected trustee board, constituted to
legally hold in trust the real estate and business affairs of the church, should
be Spirit-led, but it can never rightly fill the place of God-ordained, Spirit-
led elders and bishops. A deacon must be a true Christian in every way. We
can find the answer to these questions in the Scripture in our lesson.
MEMORY VERSE: Likewise must the deacons be grave, not double-
tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre.
—1 Timothy 3:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Proverbs 16 Right use of speech.
Tue.—Matthew 25:31-40 Service to needy.
Wed.—Romans 16:1-16 Helpers in God's work.
Thu.—1 Peter 3:10-16 Upright Christian living.
Fri.—1 Peter 4:1-11 Serving God seriously.
Devotional Reading: 1 Corinthians 12 God sets offices in church.
Personal Qualifications of a Deacon
1 Timothy 3:8-10 Likewise must the deacons—in the same way as the elders. (See Lesson 4.) The word
deacon means a regularly constituted servant. Deacons serve in much the same way as elders, but in a secondary
capacity. We might call them assistants to elders. They are to carry more of the material service such as
providing for the needs of the sick and poor, while elders look more to the spiritual needs. Yet, their service is
the same in many respects. Their character must be as holy as an elder's, a good example for all to follow. (1)
Must the deacons be grave—thoughtful, serious-minded, realizing the importance and responsibility of their
call? Both thoughts and actions should be suitable for the seriousness of the position. (2) Not double-tongued—
not talking on both sides of a subject, two-faced, hypocritical. (3) Not given to much wine—no drinker of
intoxicants. How can a person given to God be also given to wine—sold, bound, enslaved? No man can serve
two masters (Matthew 6:24). (4) Not greedy of filthy lucre—not in it for financial gain. Money cannot
satisfy, is perishable, and keeps one's eyes from the greater gain. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his
righteousness (Matthew 6:33). Needs left in God's hands, He will supply. (5) Holding the mystery of the
faith—understanding and believing the doctrine of Christ, His deity, death, resurrection, and what these
accomplish for sinners. In a pure conscience—free from guilt, forgiven, saved, justified, and holy. Not only
must deacons believe Christ's doctrine, but they must experience it. (6) Let these also first be proved—a
newly-saved, inexperienced, untrained one is not ready. Let him learn, gain experience and understanding, be
proved or tried. When he shows himself worthy and capable, let him use the office of a deacon, being found
blameless.

LESSON 5
His Family Life
1 Timothy 3:11 Even so—out of the same kind of holy life—must their wives be—if wives are to help
their husbands in spiritual work, they must be (a) grave—serious-minded about their work. (b) Not
slanderers—not gossips, talebearers, breeders of suspicion, or evil-tongued. There is nothing more devilish than
an evil tongue. Is any sin more easily fallen into than careless talking? Does any do more harm? (c) Sober—
calm, steady, self-controlled, not giddy or silly. (d) Faithful in all things—true to Jesus Christ, dependable,
trustworthy, honest in all dealings, sincere, constant. A pastor's wife of this sort is a great asset to any
congregation.
1 Timothy 3:12 (7) Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife— true to marriage vows, not a bigamist.
(8) Ruling their children and their own houses well—requiring obedience, not cruel, not slack, loving,
teaching, training and directing his children, taking the headship of the family as the husband and father should,
and guiding it in well-ordered ways.
Paul's Purpose in Writing
1 Timothy 3:13 They that have used the office of a deacon well— have followed the stated rules and been
faithful to God— purchase to themselves a good degree—earn honor with both God and men, establish a good
record—and great boldness in the faith—By practice and experience become learned in the Scriptures, wise in
spiritual matters, able in teaching or preaching, powerful in prayer, and convincing to men. What greater reward
can one seek in this life? There is no greater!
1 Timothy 3:14-15 Paul hopes to see Timothy soon, but in case of delay, he sent this letter of advice as to
how best to conduct himself, or the best action to take to set the church in order. He uses three terms to
designate the church. (1) The house of God— the temple in which God dwells. (Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter
2:5.) These people in whom God lives are His church. (2) The church of the living God. (3) The pillar and
ground of the truth. The truth is in both its foundation and its structure. The church grows out of the truth, and
the church continues to lift and spread the truth. What a great responsibility the church has to hold high the truth
that the world can see Christ, through Whom sinful souls are transformed into saints.
God's Perfect Plan of Church Government
The simple structure of the church as Christ set it up is perfect and entire, needing no addition or
remodeling. He gives to each, gifts of the Spirit to carry on the work of the church. He sets elders and deacons to
govern and direct the work. We find no higher human officers in the early church. These were led, taught, and
guided by the Holy Spirit. There is no teaching in the Bible that men with superior authority should be set over
the elders and congregations. (Matthew 20:25-26.) It was later when men, drifting from the Spirit's rule, set a
bishop over elders, then an archbishop, and so on. The Pope of Rome was the first to take the title of Bishop of
Bishops.
Deaconesses
In Romans 16:1 the word servant applied to Phoebe is the same term as is translated deacon in our lesson.
The word deaconess is not in the Bible. What would be the work and standing of such a servant?

"He that is at war with others is not at peace with himself."

LESSON 6
THE MYSTERY OF GODLINESS
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 Corinthians 2:7-12; Colossians 1:26-27;
Ephesians 1:9-10
What is the mystery of godliness? By what means can we understand it? Is it
important that we understand it? Does a person who has a Bible or a place of
worship necessarily have the Gospel? Do living with Christians or attending
Sunday school and preaching services guarantee that one knows the Gospel or
understands the mystery? (1 Corinthians 2:14.) Does knowing the words of the
Bible reveal to one the mystery? How does our text agree with the song that says,
"It is no secret what God can do?"
Salvation is a mystery to those without God's Spirit. The mystery is that God's
Son came, became flesh, died, rose, and returned to Heaven to save man from sin.
MEMORY VERSE: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh,
justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
—1 Timothy 3:16
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Psalm 25 A prayer to be taught of God.
Tue.—Matthew 13:10-17, Matthew 13:35 Reason for parables.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 4:1-6 Gospel hid to the lost.
Thu.—Ephesians 1:1-12 Purpose of the mystery revealed.
Fri.—1 Peter 1:3-13, 1 Peter 1:20 The mystery revealed.
Devotional Reading: Ephesians 3 Mystery made known to Paul.
Great Is the Mystery
1 Timothy 3:16 Without controversy—certain, without possibility of refutation—great is the mystery—
something secret, hidden, not known to all—of godliness—of Godlikeness, of making men like God. This is the
greatest plan that concerns mankind. Paul names six details of how the plan will be carried out. (1) God was
manifest in the flesh—Jesus Christ, or God the Son, became man. He took upon Himself a human body. The
Word was made flesh (John 1:14). These statements prove the deity and also the humanity of Jesus. (2)
Justified in the Spirit—was proven by the Holy Spirit to be what He claimed to be. At His baptism (John 1:32-
34), His resurrection (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 3:18), and by His miracles (John 10:25), the Spirit justified Him.
(3) Seen of angels—That angels have an interest and a part in the redemptive work of Christ is shown by their
activity in preparation for His coming, at His birth, flight to Egypt, temptation, agony, resurrection, and
ascension. They rejoice over one sinner that repenteth (Luke 15:10). They desire to look into these truths (1
Peter 1:12). (4) Preached unto the Gentiles—to non-Jews as well as Jews. It is a precious part of this mystery
that Jesus tasted death for every man, not one left out (Hebrews 2:9). (5) Believed on in the world—among the
unbelievers there are also those who believe everywhere Christ is preached. Sinners whose sins He denounces
embrace Him as their Savior. (6) Received up into glory—ascended back to Heaven from where He came. This
is all important to us. His living is the promise of our living (John 14:19). His entrance into Heaven is the
promise of our entrance. His going with His visible, human body is the promise of our going with ours. His
eternal living is the promise of ours. Praise God! These and more belong to the plan of salvation whereby sinful
people are made godly. This is truly a mystery. The world cannot understand this.

LESSON 6
A Mystery to the Unsaved
1 Corinthians 2:7-8 But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom. Hidden
because it is not understood. God's plan of salvation through Christ was ordained before the world—was
planned by God before creation of the world. God gradually made it known through His Prophets, but they
themselves did not fully understand what they wrote of Christ (Romans 16:25-26; 1 Peter 1:10-12). The fuller
revelation came with the coming of Christ. None of the princes of this world knew—earthly, natural men, those
out-side of Christ, did not know this mysterious wisdom, this plan of God (Mark 4:11). Thanks be to God! It
can be known.
The Mystery Revealed by the Spirit
1 Corinthians 2: 9-12 The things which God hath prepared for them that love him—the blessings of
salvation in this present life. Many separate verse 9 from verse 10 in the context and so misinterpret it. Man's
natural eyes, ears, and heart cannot grasp these things, but God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit. The
spirit of man knoweth the things of a man. The Spirit of God knoweth the things of God. God planned it this
way. That is why He gave us the spirit which is of God—the Holy Spirit—that we might know the things
that are freely given to us by God. Through the working of the Spirit, we can take His gift of salvation, can
experience it, grow in it, know it, feel it, and know God and Jesus Christ. Knowing the mysteries, we hold them
in our hearts. We are made stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1). As stewards, we are bound
by love and duty to teach others.
The Substance of God's Plan
Colossians 1:26-27 The riches of the glory of this mystery . . . is Christ in you. The whole plan, from
beginning to end, is to bring about the indwelling of Christ in the hearts of men. What a great mystery! God
wants us to know this. He also wants us to know the purpose for which Christ dwells in us. God tells us the
specific details of His plan that is great enough to occupy His attention from before the Creation until time shall
cease. Then the mystery of God shall be finished, not ended, but complete (Revelation 10:7).
The Goal of God's Plan
Ephesians 1:9-10 The mystery of his will . . . that in . . . the fullness of times—this is the next
dispensation which will begin at Christ's Second Coming when the world ends and time shall be no more—then
He will gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth. All
who have salvation will be brought together in one great family to dwell even in him. This includes God the
Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the angels, and all redeemed people. Then we shall be like him; for we shall
see him as he is (1 John 3:2).
Oh, how great is the mystery of godliness! Dear friend, don't miss it. Start today. Make Christ your personal
Savior.

"Man gets and forgets; God gives and forgives."
—Myron F. Boyd

LESSON 7
PROPHECY OF COMING APOSTASY
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 4:1-9; Colossians 2:8, Colossians 2:13-23
The express speaking of the Spirit names specific practices which are
the outgrowth of apostasy. Apostasy is the departure from true teaching
and beliefs. What religious systems fit the description named in our text?
Is Catholicism the only system that incurs God's wrath? Wherever men
stray from the mainstream of the Gospel, God's attitude toward it and the
result is the same. The tragic result brings a departing of God's Spirit
from a group or an individual life. What would you call the chief wrong
of the apostasy foretold here? What is meant by bodily exercise?
Apostasy in the latter times is prophesied. We must watch that we be
not led astray.
MEMORY VERSE: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
—1 Thessalonians 5:21

Some Shall Depart
1 Timothy 4:1-3 The Spirit speaketh expressly—the Holy Spirit spoke to Paul, pointedly, specifically,
clearly. In the latter times—meaning later than He spoke, in the last dispensation, the one then in its beginning
and now still continuing in these latter days—some shall depart from the faith—from the truth of Christ, the
way of salvation. Why? Because they give heed to—listen to—seducing spirits—spirits that deceive— and
doctrines of devils—evil teachings and practices. Paul names some: (1) Teaching about demons. Pagans
worshipped demons believed to be agents between gods and men, some being souls of dead humans. This
practice would be a part of the worship of those apostates. (2) Speaking lies in hypocrisy. Not being founded
on truth, they do not love truth, but follow the devil's practice of lying (John 8:44). In hypocrisy—pretending
to be good, wearing a cloak of right (Matthew 7:15-16). (3) Having their conscience seared with a hot iron.
Deadened to feeling, they sin with no remorse and seemingly little realization that it is sin. They feel no
repentance. The same hot iron of the Gospel of Christ that smoothes out the wrinkles of the hearer will sear the
conscience if unheeded. (4) Forbidding to marry. Refusing themselves to marry and requiring others to remain
single, forgetting God's Word that marriage is honorable in all (Hebrews 13:4). (5) Commanding to abstain
from meats. They make rules forbidding food at certain times or certain foods to be eaten ever or at certain

Freedom in Christ
1 Timothy 4:4-5 Every creature of God—everything created by God— is good. He called it very good
(Genesis 1:31). Nothing to be refused—that is, nothing that was made for food is to be denied or forbidden—if
received with thanksgiving. No ungrateful, arrogant reaching for God's gifts as if they belonged to us pleases
God. If accepted thankfully, food is sanctified— pure and sacred. Two things make it so. (1) The word of God.
God's Word or authority set food apart for man's use (Genesis 1:29). (2) And prayer—both prayer for God to
provide (Matthew 6:11) and thanks to Him for having done so (Romans 14:6; Ephesians 5:20).
How to Be a Good Servant
1 Timothy 4:6 Timothy was put in trust by God as a minister, a servant of God and the church. To fulfill
this trust, he must put the brethren in remembrance of these things—tell, remind, instruct, warn them of the
coming apostasy and teach them how to refuse the false and hold to the truth. Thus Timothy would show
himself nourished or taught in the words of faith and of good doctrine. Paul knew he had attained to this
place and wanted him to continue in it.
Can one be a good servant of Christ and shut his eyes to the signs of apostasy? Can one be a good watchman
and not warn the flock of these dangers? Can he be true to the Lord and the spiritual gift given him unless he
puts the brethren in remembrance of the sharp line of difference between godliness and fables? It may make one
popular to cooperate with everything and to smile at all doctrines, but it does not please God. See 2 Corinthians
Godliness Versus Bodily Exercise
1 Timothy 4:7-9 Throughout our lesson text we see two ways of life expressed. They are (1) godliness, or
Godlikeness, obeying God, living as motivated by the Spirit, and (2) bodily exercise, or outward forms and
observances, obeying man's ordinances, living as motivated by our minds and wills. The first is freedom in
Christ (John 8:36); the second is bondage to man's rules. The first is on the inside; the second, on the outside.
The first is minding the things of the Spirit; the second, minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5). The first
is living in the power of God; the second is living in one's own human strength. Godliness is profitable unto all
things. Godliness benefits in this life and also in the life to come. But bodily exercise profiteth little—is
wasted effort. Refuse profane and old wives' fables—earthly, man-made traditions and superstitions. They
lead many souls to destruction.
Colossians 2:8, Colossians 2:13-23 Even the forms and days of the Mosaic Law are of no effect since
Christ came. They were the shadow or type. Christ is the body or real substance, the antitype. Voluntary
humility is much the same as bodily exercise. By their own willpower, people afflict the physical body in
outward, material ways. They forbid touching or tasting or handling. They neglect or punish the body to gain
merit. They spend their time and energy on things that are to perish with the using— outward things. They

LESSON 8
ADVICE TO A YOUNG MINISTER
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 4:10-16
Why is it that so few of the modern ministers seem to never have seriously
read these directions stated by Paul in today's lesson text? For most, their method
of spending their time, the business and pleasures of their lives, and the
objectives that they pursue cause them to be just the opposite of what they should
be.
No other way is found in the New Testament for doing God's work than by
God's spiritual gifts. 1 Corinthians 12:1 says we should not be ignorant about
spiritual gifts. 1 Corinthians 12:18 says everyone is set in the body as God
pleases. Each has a particular place with a particular work. 1 Peter 4:10-11 says
that if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth. There is
no other way to success in God's work. Timothy ministered by means of a gift of
the Spirit. What is the way to obtain spiritual gifts?
MEMORY VERSE: Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou
shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.—1 Timothy 4:16
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Joshua 1:1-9 God's charge to Joshua.
Tue.—Ezekiel 33:1-9 Responsibility of watchmen.
Wed.—Matthew 10:16-33 Men of God can expect persecution.
Thu.—Acts 26:12-23 Paul's call to God's work.
Fri.—Romans 10 The need for God-sent preaching.
Devotional Reading: Romans 1:1-16 Ready to preach Gospel.
Laborers Suffer Reproach
1 Timothy 4:10-11 The first verse of this chapter told of a departure from the faith, from the great mystery
of godliness. Paul exhorted Timothy to press on in the way of godliness, which promises great profit both in this
life and in the next. For therefore—because we desire to preserve this way of godliness—we both labor and
suffer reproach. Paul and others like him valued the Gospel of Christ so highly that they were glad to work and
be persecuted severely because of their trust in the living God. Here the same One is called both God and
Savior, one more proof of the deity of Jesus Christ. Jesus is the God and Savior of all men—He died for all (2
Corinthians 5:15), was crucified to draw all men unto Him (John 12:32), is the Light, which lighteth every
man (John 1:9), and is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).
He is the Savior specially of those that believe. Only these actually receive salvation. Salvation is for all,
but not all have it. Read Matthew 7:14; John 3:36. These verses should settle two false teachings, (1) Limited
Atonement (that Christ died to save a limited part of mankind) and (2) Universalism (that everyone will be
saved). No, the atonement is not limited, but acceptance of it is. God wills all to be saved, but not all will repent.
These things command and teach. What things? That men should refuse false doctrine and pursue godliness,
that godliness brings blessing both now and hereafter, that salvation in Christ is of so great value as to render
unimportant any labor or persecution brought by it, and that Jesus saves from sin any and all who believe on
Him.

LESSON 8
Youth Is a Powerful Influence
1 Timothy 4:12-13 Let no man despise thy youth. Timothy was a young man, but he should not let his
youth lead him into foolish, hasty, extreme, passionate, or worldly action. This would bring the criticism that he
was too young to lead. Instead, he must be an example of the believers—show what an ideal believer is, that
others might pattern after him. In word—in what he said and what he taught, teaching the truth, the Gospel of
Christ. In conversation—in all of his conduct in all places at all times, act in a holy, Christian manner. In
charity—let the love of God within him rule his conduct. In spirit—in the inward feeling and visible attitude in
which he lived and acted. In faith—living continually with an open channel of trust reaching to God by which
to communicate with Him and receive from Him. This also includes the thought of faithfulness to God and to
the church in the trust placed in his hands. He must be a faithful steward of the mysteries of God (1
Corinthians 4:1-2). In purity—unmixed with sin, sanctified unto God, unspotted from the world, clean in
thought and action, giving no one reason to scandalize his good name.
Give attendance to reading—read the Bible, study it, let his delight be in the Law of the Lord; meditate on
it every day. Give attendance to exhortation—pass on to the people the commands of God and the importance
of obedience. And to doctrine—teach the people the truths of God, give them a solid foundation in God's Word
from which to grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior (2 Peter 3:18).
All through Bible history, in both the Old and New Testaments, there have been young people whom God
used in a mighty way. God does not consider the age of a person, but He looks at the willingness and obedience
of those He would use in His work. Let no young person feel he is too young to be of service to God. Do not be
intimidated because you are young when God has a work for you.
Serving and Continuing Faithful
1 Timothy 4:14 Neglect not the gift—the gift of the Spirit which God had placed in Timothy had (1) set
him in his particular place of service in the church and (2) given the spiritual abilities necessary to do that work.
Two actions accompanied the giving of this gift to Timothy, (1) prophecy—Word from God telling Timothy
and others of His choice of Timothy for this work and (2) the laying on of the hands of Paul and other elders (1
Timothy 1:18; 2 Timothy 1:6). Paul urged Timothy to neglect not—to develop the gift by using it, by prayer,
and listening to God.
1 Timothy 4:15-16 Meditate upon these things—think deeply and continually on the truths he read, the
great salvation of which he was steward in the Gospel, his responsibility in leading the church and winning
souls, the goals set before him, and the gift by which he did all. Give thyself wholly—not halfheartedly, but
make the service of God his one interest and concern.
Two matters Timothy was told to take heed unto: First, thyself—pay careful attention to his own life that it
please God, that he himself obey the Spirit and God's Word, and that his heart remain pure. Second, the
doctrine—watch carefully to always teach God's Word as it is, the full Gospel, unmixed with error. These
would bring two results: First, he would save himself; by remaining true to God, he would assure his final
salvation in Heaven. Second, he would save those who heard him; his holy example and teaching of truth would
bring them to God. God has chosen to give us His will in a Book. What are we doing with it?
JUST A THOUGHT
Reading is a priceless treasure and a powerful influence.

LESSON 9
CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS IN SOCIETY
Scripture Texts: 1 Timothy 5:1-8; 1 Timothy 6:1-2
As we study, we should bear in mind that even though the Book of Timothy
was written to a young pastor and is primarily advice for the carrying on of his
work, it states the basic principles for the individual Christian's success in the
society in which he lives. The only difference is in the particular circumstance
in which each is placed. So here, while Timothy may have viewed these
instructions from one position and some of us from another, still, they have an
application for every one of us.
Christian attitudes of kindness, love, and respect must be used toward all
people. We must provide for those for whose support we are responsible. Who
has the first responsibility in the care of needy ones and dependents? What
virtue is most effective in producing right relations between individuals?
MEMORY VERSE: Look not every man on his own things, but every man
also on the things of others.
—Philippians 2:4

Tue.—Psalm 78:1-8 Teaching children God's Law.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 13 The love of God in action.
Thu.—Ephesians 6:1-9 The Christian household.
Fri.—Colossians 3 Holy living.
Devotional Reading: Titus 2 Christian doctrine and conduct.
Treatment of Others
1 Timothy 5:1-2 Rebuke not—In correcting faults, wrongs, or misunderstandings, in what manner shall it
be done? Gently, tenderly, with the love one would show to one's own brother, sister, father, or mother. If in the
church, they are brothers and sisters, born of the same Father. Rebuke not . . . but entreat—with gentle
understanding, seek to persuade them to a better way. An elder here means an older man, not a church officer.
The term corresponds to the term elder women. These are to be given the loving respect due parents; the
younger ones deserve respect due brothers and sisters in a family. With all purity—Timothy, as a young
minister, must be especially careful in his conduct toward younger women, to avoid temptation to himself,
temptation to them, and suspicion on the part of others. This same standard of respect should be maintained by
all toward any of the opposite sex.
Caring for Relatives
1 Timothy 5:3-7 Honor widows that are widows indeed—accept and support those destitute of other
support. This, obviously, is speaking to the church. Then, to individuals again—if any widow has children or
nephews, let them assume the support. Thus they shew piety at home, which is a first duty, and requite their
parents—repay for the love and care they received in their helpless years. Best of all, they please God. Then,
two kinds of widows are contrasted—widows indeed and those who live in pleasure, in luxury, ease, and self-
indulgence. The first trust in God, while the others do not. The first live by continual prayer. The second are
