LESSON 9
dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), spiritually dead, while living physically. Material comforts and
worldly pleasures dull the sense of dependence upon God. These things give in charge—teach to the people
that they may obey and be blameless.
Today the increasing number of elderly people and the large number of working wives has brought a growth
in the custom of placing elderly parents and relatives in nursing centers. Does this fulfill one's duty to them?
How much weight should each of these bear upon the decision of what to do—The wife's job? The disposition
of the aged one? Adults' desire for freedom? Finances? Size of house? What benefits may come to each
household member when a dependent is cared for? To live in pleasure, in self-indulgence, and to please self is to
be dead spiritually. This is true of an individual or a church or a nation.
Duty of Supporting Own Family
1 Timothy 5:8 A man must provide for his own—any relatives for whom he is the main means of support.
Specially for those of his own house—his immediate family, wife, children, parents, or those under his roof.
These are his first responsibility. Then he should reach to other dependents as far as he is able. To shirk his duty
is to deny the faith, to sin against his Christian profession. Worse than an infidel or unbeliever, for even
unbelievers generally fill their responsibility for their own.
This is part of the nurture and admonition of the Lord in which children should be brought up. Read
Ephesians 6:4. This is part of our training them in respect for their elders, in faithful discharge of
responsibilities, in self-sacrifice rather than self-indulgence. It is not fair to a child to let him grow up pampered
and free from responsibility, then expect him to assume the duties of adulthood. The duties of our lesson are for
adults and children alike.
Relation of Servants and Masters
1 Timothy 6:1-2 Should a saint be a servant under the yoke? Not under the yoke and bondage of slavery,
but under the yoke of Jesus his Master. He should not rebel against serving those who have the authority over
him. Such action would cause blasphemy or unjust criticism of God and his doctrine. We are not living in a
day of slavery as when this letter was written, but this does not give reason for the saint to give less than his best
to those for whom he is employed. He should give a full day's work for a full day's pay. The unsaved always
watch Christians and expect a higher degree of patience and work ethics from them. If a master is a Christian
also, the servant must not feel that his spiritual equality is reason for a lesser effort, or reason to take an
advantage of him—despise them, because they are brethren. Rather, he must serve faithfully because his
master is a beloved brother, a partaker of the benefit of salvation. Being united with him in Christ, he serves
from love (Galatians 5:13). Work as unto the Lord and not to man. Read Ephesians 6:5-9.
JUST A THOUGHT
After a man makes his mark in the world, a lot of people will come around with erasers.

LESSON 10
CONDUCT OF CHRISTIANS IN THE CHURCH
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 5:9-25
The choice of who should support the needy in Paul's day was between the church
and relatives. It seems that governments of that time had no welfare programs. Care for
the unfortunate is a product of love and is a peculiarity of God's people. Some
governments have now taken over much welfare work. This is good and bad. Good, in
that there are many needy ones who the church cannot help materially. But bad, in that
the church has often been satisfied to leave it to them. There are some who are the
government's responsibility. There are others who are the responsibility of relatives.
But the church is responsible for its own. The church should provide for its needy ones,
respect and support its leaders, and keep itself clean from sin.
MEMORY VERSE: Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or
three witnesses.
—1 Timothy 5:19
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Acts 6:1-7 Support of the widows.
Tue.—Romans 12 Living in the body of Christ.
Wed.—1 Corinthians 9:1-15 Support of ministers.
Thu.—2 Corinthians 6 Faithful workers.
Fri.—Titus 3 Living as Christians
Devotional Reading: Hebrews 13 Christian Obligations.
Qualifications of Accepted Widows
1 Timothy 5:9-10 Let not a widow be taken into the number—It is evident here and in following verses
that support of needy widows is meant. The qualifications set for them are: (1) At least threescore years old—
an age of settled character. (2) Having been the wife of one man—one at a time, true to a husband all of his
life. Second marriage after the death of a husband is not prohibited here, being consistent with 1 Timothy 5:14
and Romans 7:3. (3) Having a record of good works—Christian deeds. (4) Have brought up children—not
necessarily children born to her, and been a good mother to teach and train them for God. I have known a
number of saintly women who did much to raise children for God who never bore children of their own. (5)
Have lodged strangers—used hospitality (Hebrews 13:1-2). In times and places where public accommodations
are scanty, this virtue is very necessary. (6) Have washed the saints' feet—participated in the ordinance Jesus
established. This includes also a life filled with the deeds of loving kindness and humility which the ordinance
symbolizes (Colossians 3:12-14). (7) Have relieved the afflicted—given help to the sick, poor, friendless,
discouraged, or any needy. (8) Diligently followed every good work—this supplies everything remaining for
well-rounded Christian practice. Such are the widows to be provided for by the church.
Widows to Be Rejected
1 Timothy 5:11-16 Some widows were not to be accepted on this list. Younger widows refuse. Why?
Because, being young, they would desire to remarry and fail to marry in the Lord, as the Bible instructs (1
Corinthians 7:39) and thus turn from the obligations of this special position. They would wax wanton against
Christ—throw off the restraints, literally live as they please. Having damnation—not that of hell, but blame
© 2015 Church of God, Inc.

LESSON 10
and condemnation for having backslid from their commitment. They cast off their first faith or promise. They
would learn to be: (1) Idle—being supported by the church, they would feel no need to work. (2) Wandering
about—not keepers at home (Titus 2:5). (3) Tattlers—telling to all what they heard from house to house
(Proverbs 18:8). (4) Busybodies—meddling, always managing the business of others but never their own. (5)
Speaking things which they ought not—all kinds of evil words. Idle words are bound to bring in some evil.
What a charge to young widows! But Paul spoke from what he had seen—some are already turned aside from
duties in the church after Satan. He advises these widows to marry the second time, bear children, guide the
house, and thus avoid just blame.
Duties of Elders
1 Timothy 5:17-18 Support—elders that rule well . . . especially they who labor in the word and
doctrine. Those who care well for the spiritual needs of the flock and teach, explain, preach, and apply God's
Word are to receive double honor—due respect and greater financial reward. Their work requires more care
and expense than does one that holds a lesser position. Paul quotes Scripture as authority in 1 Corinthians 9:7-
14 and Luke 10:7.
1 Timothy 5:19-20 Accusations—Against an elder receive not an accusation. He who assumes any
service of leadership invites criticism of it. An elder must at times use corrective measures which may arouse
resentment. No accusation must be received unless fully proved by two or three witnesses. If proved, the
offender must be rebuked before all to keep the church clear of approving and fostering sin.
Elders' Duties Concerning Individuals
Partiality—So prone are we to let our human feelings guide our actions in spiritual work that Paul reminds
Timothy that the Father, the Son and the elect angels are seeing his actions. He charged him to use no partiality,
not to prefer one more than another, either in support given, in rebuke of sin, or in favors shown. God is no
respecter of persons; neither should we be.
1 Timothy 5:22-25 Sudden approval—God ordains elders, or chooses and places them (1 Corinthians
12:18). Then by prayer and laying on of hands, Christian leaders formally acknowledge God's ordination (1
Timothy 4:14). This must not be done suddenly—not without knowledge of the man's qualifications and call
nor until he has proven himself worthy (1 Timothy 3:6-10). To do so would be taking part in the sin of putting
an unfit man into sacred office and also to being a part of any harm he might do there. Keep thyself pure—free
from any action of defiling the Church of God with unholy hands and uncalled leaders. Also, here lays the
responsibility to preach and live the truth before all men. Either the sins or the good works of some candidates
are open beforehand—easily seen. Those of others follow after—are seen only after careful investigation.
Drink no longer water— alone—but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake . . . Timothy's health was
necessary to keep him serving the church as an elder. The water was very unsuitable for drinking, and Paul
found it necessary to remind Timothy to add a little juice from the fruit of the vine to make the water healthier
for his body. Paul did not advocate the drinking of intoxicants. This would be unthinkable. Read Paul's writings
in Ephesians 5:18 and 1 Corinthians 6:10.
JUST A THOUGHT
The drinking man commits suicide on the installment plan.

LESSON 11
FALSE RICHES
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 6:3-10
Is one right in believing that health and wealth
compose Christianity? When you drive through a
community and see well kept houses and big, well
filled barns, is that Christianity? Is it right or wrong to
have good things and a prosperous business? In what
does the right or wrong lie? In the love of money, lies
the wrong. The right attitude toward possessions,
money, and necessary provisions is the difference
between them being a blessing or a curse. Material
riches are temporary. To love them is sin.
This lesson begins with two classes of people and traces their lives from the beginnings down through to
their different ends. In these verses, main attention is given to the evil. The next lesson considers the righteous.
MEMORY VERSE: And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.—1 Timothy 6:8
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Deuteronomy 8:10-20 The giver of riches.
Tue.—2 Kings 5:20-27 Punishment for covetousness.
Wed.—Ecclesiastes 5:9-16 Money does not satisfy.
Thu.—Matthew 19:16-29 Possessions can be a hindrance.
Fri.—Luke 12:13-21 A rich fool.
Devotional Reading: James 5:1-9 Moth-eaten garments.
Christ's Way Versus the World's Way
1 Timothy 6:3-5 If any man teach otherwise—other than Paul had just outlined in the previous verses.
Paul taught the Words of Christ and said (verse 2), These things teach and exhort. Paul urged in similar words
a number of times through this Book. But some—sinners—would not consent or agree with Christ's Words,
with doctrine . . . according to godliness. Those people, because they started off from the wrong foundation
(their own human thoughts) and set before them the wrong principle, are filled with all kinds of evil—pride,
ignorance, love of arguing over questions about the Word, twisting meanings and splitting hairs, name-calling
and suspicion. Their minds are corrupt and filled with evil thoughts. Not taking the way of love, refusing the
truth, they envy and fight and dispute. They reject the principle of godliness and take that of gain—thinking
gain is godliness. They seek money and earthly possessions instead of things of God. Paul said, from such
withdraw thyself.
Godliness and Contentment
1 Timothy 6:6-8 The natural, unsaved, worldly man lives by the false principle that gain is godliness, but
Paul says the exact opposite is true—godliness . . . is great gain. Riches do not make one good, but godliness
does make one rich in a better way. Godliness with contentment—because one has the godliness he most
desires, he is contented with whatever he has of less value. Material comforts and possessions last only for this
life. We do not bring them in with us, and we cannot take them out with us. If we have food and raiment—
clothing and shelter—it is enough. Temporary things do only for a temporary life. For the eternal life of the soul,

LESSON 11
better and lasting things are needed. It requires but little of this world's goods to satisfy a person who realizes he
is not a citizen of this world, but of Heaven. Truly rich is the one who has godliness in his soul, food on his
table, raiment and shelter for his body, and desires nothing more.
Covetousness Is the Way Down
1 Timothy 6:9-10 There is a very different result for those that will be rich. This desire is covetousness, the
wish to get and to have, not to give, but to keep. One filled with this desire falls. The way is down, down, down.
First, into temptation—they are tempted to selfishness, pride, stinginess, dishonesty, lying, etc. Further down
into a snare—a trap with which Satan deceives and binds one in habits he never intended to practice. Down into
lusts where chains of Satan are bound tighter and tighter. Foolish lusts which bring no lasting good, no spiritual
blessing, and no soul-satisfaction. Hurtful lusts which lead to sins listed in preceding verses, make the heart
hard, unloving, and selfish, and shut out God's voice. Finally, these lusts drown men in destruction—cut the
line of communication with God and destroy their souls—and perdition—hereafter cast them into hell forever.
Not much gain on this downward road, is there? For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole
world, and lose his own soul? (Mark 8:36). The love of money—not money, which can do much good, but
the love of it in the heart—is the root of all evil, or all kinds of evil, as were named. Coveting it causes one to
err from the faith—to miss the mark—and to pierce oneself through with many sorrows. Such is the end of
those who set gain rather than godliness and things more than God as their goal in life. Riches profit not in the
day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death (Proverbs 11:4).
The Deceitfulness of Riches
Does it seem that our text is too severe with a lot of nice people? People who dress well, eat well, live in
luxury are generally respected. To gain these and money besides seems to most to be a praiseworthy goal.
Worldly riches deceive souls and cause them to feel that they are rich when they are truly poor. This goal is not
enough. That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15). Often
the rich are looked up to rather than the godly person. Why? Because there is a deception in worldly riches.
A story is told of a certain man who died. His obituary stated that "his chief ambition had been to own his
own home, and he realized his ambition." Yet, even as that was being written, he lay dead. The earthly home
was no longer his, and he had no greater ambition. Still, people said he had done well. Were they deceived? Was
he? Are you deceived, dear one?
JUST A THOUGHT
Don't expect a bargain when you are shopping for sinful pursuits.

LESSON 12
TRUE RICHES
Scripture Text: 1 Timothy 6:11-21
The rich are to use their riches in good works that they may lay hold on eternal
life. Will these works save? No. Does each good deed add merit to one's account to
be applied against one's sins, as some teach? No. Not by works of righteousness
which we have done (Titus 3:5). No, works cannot save. We are saved by the riches
of Christ's goodness, God's grace (Romans 2:4; Ephesians 1:7). We have
redemption through the blood of Christ (Colossians 1:14). Where then do works
find a place? They are an expression of faith. Faith without works is dead. Works
indicate the quality of one's inner life. Every man will be judged according to his
works. God sees both heart and deed. We can have true riches without a dime in our pocket. Read 2
Corinthians 6:10.
To know and obey God is true riches both in this life and in the one to come.
MEMORY VERSE: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not high minded, nor trust in
uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy.
—1 Timothy 6:17
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Psalm 92 The blessing of the Lord.
Tue.—Luke 12:31-40 Treasure in the Heavens.
Wed.—2 Corinthians 8:1-15 A church rich in giving.
Thu.—Philippians 4:6-19 Looking to God to supply needs.
Fri.—Revelation 3:14-22 Gold tried in the fire.
Devotional Reading: Matthew 6:19-34 Incorruptible treasures.
The Right Way to Go
1 Timothy 6:11 Flee these things; and follow after. Here are two ways to go. Here are the same two lines
of doctrine we studied in the last lesson—one, the Words of our Lord Jesus and the other, human ideas, or one,
the way of righteousness, godliness, faith . . . and the other, the way of sin. Now, Paul says, flee one of these
and follow after the other. Flee, run for your life, from the love of money and the many sins that go with it. This
sin, the will to be rich, to gain the things of this world, is a strong and widespread temptation. Preacher and
people alike are subject to it. Flee it; it is a matter of life or death. Money, of course, cannot bring satisfaction to
the soul. Now the consideration turns to the right way, the way of Christ. Pursue it with your heart, soul, mind,
and strength. Follow righteousness—obey the Lord from the heart, love His commandments, hate sin.
Godliness—be like God, be holy, let Christ live in you. Faith—believe God, keep the channel of
communication open between you and God. Love—have the love of God in the heart, exercise that love, love
God and men. Patience—endure calmly and faithfully any work, hardship, misunderstanding, or persecution.
Meekness —be gentle, consider others ahead of yourself, and be submissive to God and to right in everything.
Fight the Good Fight
1 Timothy 6:12 Fight—Timothy was fighting with Satan to gain eternal life. He had already been a
witness to the truth of the Gospel and to his own faithfulness to it before many witnesses. The way of Christ
was a much persecuted way there. Christians professed Christ at risk of losing all they possessed, even their
lives. Timothy had suffered persecution and imprisonment and held true (Hebrews 13:23). Timothy fought

against persecutors as well as spirits. Today our greatest battle is against deceiving spirits (Ephesians 6:11-12),
spirits which lead us to believe we are right when we are wrong, that we can do wrong and get by. Our battle is
truly a daily fight of faith—our faith in God. Lay hold on eternal life—a better prize than earthly contests can
ever offer. The prize can be gained. Read 2 Timothy 4:6-7.
A Solemn Charge
1 Timothy 6:13-16 Here Paul lays a solemn charge on Timothy—binds him under obligation. He calls God
and Christ as witnesses, reminding Timothy that they see how he fulfills his duty. God, who quickeneth—He
has the power of life. Christ endured His suffering and death without sin and convinced Pilate of His
righteousness. Timothy was told what to do and the purpose of it. Keep this commandment—this Gospel—
without spot. Pass it on pure and unchanged. Unrebukeable—obey it so fully that no guilt can be found in him.
How long? This Gospel and this record are to be kept for all generations until Jesus comes again. The purpose is
to be ready for His coming. In his times he shall shew—or He will appear at the appointed time, which no man
knows (Mark 13:32). Who is He? Our Lord Jesus Christ. In the description that follows is the greatest
exaltation that human language can voice. Can any read it and doubt that Jesus is God? He is blessed—favored
of God; only Potentate— only ruler with all power and authority; the King above all kings; Lord above all
lords; only One with immortality—with inherent eternal life, Who cannot die; dwelling in the light which no
man can approach—a glory far beyond man's comprehension; no man . . . can see—finite man is incapable of
seeing infinite God (John 1:18). Jacob and Moses saw a manifestation of God in Genesis 32:30 and Exodus
33:11. This greatest, highest One will have honor and power everlasting—forever and ever.
The Right Use of Riches
1 Timothy 6:17-19 Some people are rich in this world. Having wealth is not sin. Loving it, trusting in it,
using it selfishly is. Timothy was to charge the rich—by teaching them their responsible duty. What was he to
tell them? (1) Be not high-minded—not proud, overbearing, for riches do not make one better. (2) Do not trust
in uncertain riches—they can do nothing spiritually for us; they can soon vanish. (3) Trust in God—He lives,
He gives us all things, can give all spiritual blessings. (4) Do good, that they be rich in good works. What
works? To distribute, to communicate. This is to give to those who need, and to give for the spread of the
Gospel. Thus they lay up in store true riches (Matthew 6:19-21). These are a good foundation for the time to
come—the Judgment and the next or heavenly dispensation. This record will please God and help to obtain the
greatest riches, eternal life.
Paul's Plea to Timothy
1 Timothy 6:20-21 O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust. What was committed to
Timothy? The Gospel, both to keep in his own heart and pass on to others by use of the spiritual gifts he had
received. Timothy was in danger of losing it. Everyone is in this danger as long as we are in the world in reach
of Satan's temptations. What might steal his faith? Profane and vain babblings—earthly, human ideas of those
who know nothing of the spiritual things of God. Oppositions of science falsely so called—not true science, but
philosophies that oppose the truth of God. Some professing—adopting these false ideas— have erred—have
turned from the faith, from the truth of the Gospel. But Timothy, avoid these things. Grace be with thee—the
life of God in you to keep you from the wrong and to keep you in the truth.

LESSON 13
RICHES—FORTUNE OR MISFORTUNE?
Scripture Text: Mark 10:17-31
We have studied Paul's teaching concerning true and false riches. In this
lesson we take notice of one portion of Scripture in which Jesus deals with this
subject. Jesus spoke of riches in many places throughout the New Testament.
He considered it very important in the Christian's progress. He taught that to
obtain eternal life is the greatest pursuit. Love of material possessions shuts
out one from God. Not only must our actions be right, but our hearts must be
changed. God rewards both here and hereafter for everything left behind for
His sake. True disciples of Christ will be persecuted.
MEMORY VERSE: How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the
kingdom of God!—Mark 10:23b
DAILY READINGS:
Mon.—Deuteronomy 8:10-18 Gratitude for riches.
Tue.—James 1:9-11; James 5:1-9 Vanity of riches.
Wed.—1 Timothy 6:7-12, 1 Timothy 6:17-19 Advice to the rich.
Thu.—Romans 12:1-8 Giving selves to the Lord.
Fri.—Philippians 3:4-11 Paul's denial of self for Christ.
Devotional Reading: Isaiah 55 The great invitation.
Seek Eternal Life
Mark 10:17-18 Jesus and His disciples walked toward Jerusalem where He would be put to death. There
came one running, and kneeled to him. His running indicates determined urgency to overtake Jesus before He
was gone. Kneeling indicates respect and humility. He was seeking the best gift man can attain—eternal life.
Matthew's account (Matthew 19:16) tells us that he asked, What good thing shall I do ... ? The way to God is
not by good works or accomplishments or sufferings. No! Believing rather than doing opens the way to God.
The heart must be changed. This man (Matthew tells us he was young and Luke that he was a ruler) called Jesus,
Good Master. Jesus answered, Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is God. The
thing that made Jesus good was the only thing that makes any other person good, a work of God's goodness in
the heart, making one a son of God.
When the Bible speaks of eternal life, it means not only its quantity—endless—but also its quality—
heavenly. It is that life which God has. It is the life that is in His Son Jesus (1 John 5:11-12). It is the life that
He gives to His people (Galatians 2:20). It is holy and ever growing. It cannot cease to be, but it can depart
from us if we let sin in. It is the greatest treasure. Seek it above all else.
Jesus Tells the Way
Mark 10:19-21 Jesus first pointed him to the Law given through Moses. Keeping it is not enough to save
one (Romans 3:28; Romans 8:3), and Jesus wanted the man to realize this from his own experience of trying to
keep it and yet remaining unsatisfied and without eternal life. Jesus beholding him loved him—because He
loved him, He told him the truth of his condition. One thing thou lackest—he had not left all, he did not love
God with all his heart, soul, mind, and strength. He still loved himself and the world. Go ... sell ... and give ...
and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take ... and follow me. To supply his lack, he must fully

surrender, be willing to sell all, give away the proceeds, take the way of sacrifice, and follow Jesus. He would
have far greater treasure than before (Matthew 6:19-20; Mark 8:34-36).
Riches a Hindrance
Mark 10:22-27 The young man made a wrong decision. He went away grieved—offended by the Words of
Jesus. He went away from Jesus, peace, joy, a life of service to Christ, and endless bliss in Heaven with God. He
went to sadness, grief, remorse, despair, darkness, and death. In just a short time, he lost his riches to the Roman

have an intoxicating charm that drives one to get more and more. It is not only those that have money who love
it. Some of the poorest people are bound by the power of the love of riches. We call riches a fortune. In the light
of the Bible, would they better be called a misfortune? The disciples were astonished at Jesus' Words! It is
easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle ... He compared it to a rich man entering the kingdom. It
is impossible with men. Jesus said it plainly. Only God can cleanse the love and trust of money from a rich
man's heart and fit him into the kingdom.
The Reward for Dedication
Mark 10:28-31 Jesus had promised the young man treasure in heaven if he obeyed. Peter was reminded of
his experience. What would the disciples have for giving up all for Jesus? An hundredfold now and eternal
life hereafter. For giving up family, the dedicated one has loving spiritual brothers and sisters. For giving up
possessions, he has his needs supplied by God through His people. The joy from these and in the world to come
is immeasurable riches. But with persecutions. Satan and the world always oppose those who go all the way
with Jesus. First shall be last ... Jesus explains His meaning of this verse in the parable of Matthew 20:1-16.
Equal riches are for all who qualify.
The Consecrated Life
We may hold in our possession many things—material, physical, mental, and spiritual. To follow Christ,
some of these must be sacrificed, others dedicated. Anything that would hinder the full life of Christ in us must
be left, cast aside, sacrificed. Those things that can be used in His service must be presented to Him, fully
yielded, dedicated. We must dedicate ourselves to use them at His Holy Spirit's direction. The child of God
consecrates his possessions, hands, tongue, mind, abilities, and all for God's use.
Since money can become so destructive to character, if used without reference to Christian ideals, it
becomes very important that every Christian be well acquainted with the Gospel teachings on this matter. The
Christian life involves Christian stewardship. No matter how prominent we may appear in the picture, we must
realize that everything we have has been given to us either directly or indirectly by God. One must make a friend
of money and thus keep money from becoming his enemy. He must recognize money as a servant and never
allow it to become his master. Here is a great truth—we get out of life what we put into it. For God loveth a
cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7b).
JUST A THOUGHT
The spirit in which we give is more important than the gift itself.
